The Problem, the Motivation, and the Solution

The problem: the grid changed at the edges, but the signals didn't

For most of the last century a distribution grid was a one-way pipe: energy flowed from the transmission system (operated by the TSO, the transmission system operator) down through a substation into a radial feeder (operated by the DSO, the distribution system operator) and out to passive consumers. Planning reflected that: the TSO planned its network, the DSO planned its network, and the interface between them was a fixed injection point that each side treated as an exogenous boundary condition.

That world is gone. Rooftop PV turns consumers into prosumers who export at midday. Batteries shift energy in time. Thermostatic loads (air conditioning, refrigeration), deferrable loads (washers, EV charging), and interruptible loads can all flex — if anyone gives them a reason to. The physical consequences are locational and temporal: reverse power flows, overvoltage on sunny feeders at noon, congestion on specific branches at specific hours, voltage sag at the far end of a feeder in the evening peak.

Yet the price most prosumers see is a flat tariff (or a flat feed-in tariff for PV export). A flat tariff carries no information about where the prosumer sits on the feeder or when their consumption stresses the network. Every prosumer's optimal response to a flat price is the same regardless of network conditions — so their aggregate behavior is uncoordinated with the physics, and the DSO is left to absorb congestion and voltage violations that better-timed, better-located flexibility could have avoided. The thesis behind this framework was motivated by exactly this situation in a Latin American context: rising DER/PV penetration, tariffs that do not reflect real costs, and prosumer proliferation causing congestion and voltage issues with no dynamic signal to coordinate the thousands of devices involved.

The same disconnect repeats one level up, at the TSO–DSO interface. A DSO that invests in flexibility (batteries, aggregators, control) can import the same total energy with a much less volatile profile — which means the TSO needs less transmission reinforcement to serve it. But if the two operators plan separately, nobody prices that trade-off, and the value of distribution-side flexibility to the transmission system is simply lost. The TSO–DSO interface is where the value leaks out.

The motivation: let prices do the coordinating

Transactive energy is the idea that the coordination problem above should be solved by an economic signal rather than by direct control: publish a price that varies by node and by hour, and let each prosumer's home energy-management system optimize against it. If the price is right — if it internalizes losses, congestion, and voltage constraints at each bus \(j\) and hour \(t\) — then thousands of self-interested devices collectively reproduce what a central network operator would have dispatched, without the operator ever touching a device.

The key question is what "right" means, and this is where convex optimization gives an answer that is principled rather than ad hoc. In a convex market-clearing problem, the dual variable (Lagrange multiplier) of a nodal power-balance constraint is the marginal value of energy at that node and hour. That object — a distribution-level locational marginal price, or DLMP — is the natural generalization of wholesale locational marginal pricing down into the distribution network. Charge it, and each prosumer's private optimum aligns with the social optimum. This framework calls its day-ahead incarnation the DADP (day-ahead dynamic price), written \(\lambda_j[t]\) throughout this guide.

The theory being implemented: a two-layer framework

This repository implements the two-layer theory from J.P. Palacios' PhD thesis (UNSJ/CONICET, 2022; companion paper IET GTD 2019) together with the PSR N1–N2 expansion note that extends it to investment planning.

Layer 1 — Operational: day-ahead dynamic distribution pricing

The operational layer is a single-level, convex, cooperative social-welfare maximization over a 24-hour day-ahead horizon on a radial distribution feeder. One important framing correction up front, because the thesis's own narrative can mislead: although the story is told hierarchically (the DSO "leads" by designing a price, prosumers "follow" by responding), the operational mathematics is not a bilevel game or MPEC. It is one convex program, decomposed by dual methods — and the price falls out of the duality, not out of a leader's strategy.

The ingredients:

  • Prosumer devices — thermostatic, deferrable, interruptible loads and PV+battery systems, each with a concave quadratic utility (or convex cost) and linear dynamics (indoor temperature, battery state of charge, energy windows). A KKT argument in the thesis proves the battery needs no charge/discharge binary — the whole device library is convex, binary-free (thesis eqs. 3.2–3.23).
  • Aggregators — one per load bus \(j\), rolling up their houses' devices into a nodal net power \(p_{ag_j}[t]\) and an aggregate utility \(U_{ag_j}\).
  • The network — the Baran–Wu branch-flow (DistFlow) model on the radial feeder: branch flows \(P_{ij}[t], Q_{ij}[t]\), squared voltages \(v_j[t]\), squared currents \(\ell_{ij}[t]\), impedances \(r_{ij}, x_{ij}\), with voltage bounds \(V^2_{\min} \le v_j \le V^2_{\max}\) and apparent-power (congestion) limits. The one nonconvex equation, \(\ell_{ij} = (P_{ij}^2 + Q_{ij}^2)/v_i\), is relaxed to the second-order-cone inequality \[ \ell_{ij}[t] \;\ge\; \frac{P_{ij}[t]^2 + Q_{ij}[t]^2}{v_i[t]}, \] and a parallel loss-less LinDistFlow constraint copy (the Gan–Low exactness device, thesis eqs. 3.43–3.45) makes the relaxation provably tight at the optimum on radial feeders — so the convex solution is the true AC solution, not a fiction.
  • The objective — social welfare: total prosumer utility minus the DSO's purchase cost at the wholesale (MEM) price \(\lambda_0[t]\) at the substation bus \(j=0\), the TSO–DSO frontier: \[ \max \;\; \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}} U_{ag_j}(p_{ag_j}) \;-\; \sum_{t=1}^{T} \lambda_0[t]\, p_0[t] \qquad \text{(thesis eq. 3.38)}. \]

The price is then not an extra ingredient at all. The DADP \(\lambda_j[t]\) is the dual of the nodal active-power balance constraint (thesis eq. 3.31) at bus \(j\), hour \(t\). At the substation it coincides with \(\lambda_0[t]\); at every other bus it is \(\lambda_0[t]\) plus network uplift — marginal losses, congestion rent, and voltage-constraint terms — which the framework decomposes explicitly. The thesis additionally solves this problem distributedly: an ADMM/dual-ascent scheme splits it into per-node aggregator subproblems (AGR-OPT) and one network subproblem (DSO-OPT), with the coupling price updated as \(\lambda_j \leftarrow \lambda_j + \rho\, R_{p,j}\) each iteration (\(\rho\) the penalty, \(R_{p,j}\) the nodal power mismatch). At convergence the ADMM coupling price is the centralized dual — a fact this framework verifies numerically rather than assumes.

Layer 2 — Planning: TSO–DSO investment as a Stackelberg–Nash game

The planning layer (from the PSR note) asks the investment question the operational layer makes quantifiable: a distributor can either import volatilely and force transmission reinforcement, or invest in flexibility \(x_{inv}\) and import smoothly. Here the game structure is real, not conceptual: each distributor is a leader choosing flexibility investment and an import profile \(z[t]\) through the TSO–DSO interconnection, anticipating the transmission system's reinforcement-cost response (the follower). The follower's marginal reinforcement cost appears as \(\pi[t]\), the dual of the interconnection coupling constraint — the planning-layer sibling of the DADP. The bilevel problem is solved by Benders decomposition (the follower's value function is built up from cuts \(\alpha \ge w^k + \sum_t \pi^k[t](z[t] - z^k[t])\)), and with multiple distributors sharing a corridor, a Nash equilibrium among the leaders is computed by Gauss–Seidel diagonalization — each distributor best-responds in turn until nobody moves.

The two layers compose naturally: the operational engine plays the role of the planning layer's lower-level oracle (import profile in, operating cost and coupling dual out), and the linking price chain is \(\lambda_j[t] \leftrightarrow \pi[t]\) at the interface.

The solution: what this framework actually is

TSODSO.jl is a Julia + JuMP research framework — a reproducible computational bench for this theory, built for a PhD and its collaborators. Its core value, stated as the project's own north star:

A researcher can express a scenario and a model variant declaratively, run it end-to-end with an open-source solver, and get trustworthy, reproducible results and prices — with every model assumption documented and every layer swappable.

Three design commitments follow from that sentence, and they shape everything in this guide:

  • Prices are never postulated, always recovered from duals. Every price in the framework — the DADP \(\lambda_j[t]\), the reactive component \(\mu_j[t]\), the planning dual \(\pi[t]\) — is read off a named constraint of a solved convex program. And because a dual is only meaningful when the relaxation behind it is tight, the framework refuses to return a price when its exactness certificate fails, rather than returning a plausible-looking number.
  • Every layer is swappable. The power-flow formulation, the device models, the solver, and the solve strategy (centralized vs. ADMM) are independent seams. Swapping one never requires editing another — the architecture section shows how.
  • Every model claim is validated, and reported honestly. The SOCP relaxation is certified against an independent nonconvex AC oracle; the planning game's role conventions are certified against MPEC reformulations; results carry provenance (git commit, seed, environment); and negative findings are shipped as findings. Two headline examples: the framework discovered that the SOC relaxation is genuinely inexact in the thesis's own high-PV overvoltage regime (a citable result, later addressed with a dedicated restricted formulation), and its reproduction of the thesis's headline result is honestly labeled directional-only — the DSO-surplus sign flip reproduces on public data, the +25% welfare magnitude does not.

Honest scope notes, up front: the core model is balanced positive-sequence (no unbalanced three-phase), the exactness guarantee is for radial feeders (meshed networks are a separate rung with their own certificate), all device models are convex and binary-free by construction, and the wholesale price \(\lambda_0[t]\) is exogenous and deterministic in the base model (uncertainty is handled by a dedicated stochastic rung). These are the theory's own assumptions, carried over deliberately and documented at each point of use.

The rest of this guide walks the framework the way it was built: the architecture and its abstraction ladder, then each mechanism — network model, devices, welfare solve, pricing, ADMM, planning game, and the research extensions — derived step by step, ending with the experiment harness that ties a declarative scenario to a stored, provenance-stamped result, and the validation machinery that makes the results trustworthy.

Where it lives: the project charter is .planning/PROJECT.md; the public summary is README.md; the theory extractions with equation numbers are .planning/research/THEORY-thesis.md and .planning/research/THEORY-papers.md.
See it run: the docs site's Home page and the rung ladder it indexes — every model page executes its real solver entrypoint during the docs build, so every rendered number is a genuine solve.

How the Framework Is Built

Two layers, one bench

The framework's shape follows the theory's shape. There is an operational layer (convex welfare maximization on a branch-flow network; DADP \(\lambda_j[t]\) as the dual of the nodal balance; centralized and ADMM solves) and a planning layer (Stackelberg Benders loops per distributor; Nash by Gauss–Seidel diagonalization; coupling flow \(z[t]\) with dual \(\pi[t]\)). The planning layer consumes the operational layer through one narrow interface — an operational oracle: fix an import profile \(z\), solve the operational problem, return its cost and the coupling dual. Around both layers sit a data layer (feeders, seeded profiles), a pricing/accounting layer, an experiment harness, and a validation battery.

But the more useful way to understand the codebase is not as a stack of layers — it is as a ladder.

The abstraction ladder is the architecture

The framework was built rung by rung, from a toy problem to the full research frontier, with a hard rule: every rung is a complete, runnable, validated end-to-end solve, and the interfaces introduced at a low rung must survive unchanged at the higher rungs. This is a pedagogical device (you can learn the framework by climbing) and an architectural discipline at the same time: if the SOCP rung had needed different device or pricing interfaces than the LinDistFlow rung, the seams were wrong. The published documentation mirrors the ladder one-to-one — each rung is a literate page whose solves execute during the docs build.

RungWhat it addsTheory anchor
0Toy DC problem — the architectural spine: solver factory, model context, status gate, first dual read—
1–2LinDistFlow linearized network; \(\lambda_j\) picks up loss/voltage structurethesis 3.31–3.33, 3.43
3SOCP Convex Branch Flow + LinDistFlow exactness copy; the independent AC-exactness oracle; the convex prosumer device library and the GLB-CVX welfare solvethesis 3.39, 3.43–3.45; 3.2–3.23, 3.38
4DADP/DLMP extraction + 4-way decomposition (energy / loss / congestion / voltage), welfare and surplus accounting, FIT baselinethesis 3.31, 3.46–3.47
5ADMM decomposition (AGR-OPT / DSO-OPT, dual ascent in \(\lambda_j\), adaptive \(\rho\)), cross-validated against the centralized optimumthesis 3.46–3.47
6Single-distributor Stackelberg via hand-rolled Benders, certified against BilevelJuMP MPEC reductionsPSR N1–N2 note

Two further pages sit beside rung 3 rather than above it: the overvoltage-capable restriction (a Gan–Low OPF-m shadow-voltage formulation for the high-PV regime where the plain SOCP relaxation is provably inexact) and the SOC relaxation applicability maps that chart where the exactness guarantee holds. They exist because the ladder's own validation machinery found the boundary — more on that in the validation section.

The seams: what you can swap without touching anything else

The project's extensibility requirement is concrete: a researcher must be able to swap the power-flow model, the device models, the objective, and the solve strategy independently. Four seams deliver that.

1. The power-flow seam: AbstractPowerFlow and contribute!

Every network formulation is a subtype of AbstractPowerFlow implementing one contract: 

abstract type AbstractPowerFlow end

# A formulation writes its per-bus, per-hour branch/voltage terms into the shared
# nodal-balance residual registry held by the ModelContext:
function contribute!(pf::AbstractPowerFlow, ctx, feeder; T::Int = 1) end

The trick is where the terms go: a formulation adds its expressions into a shared residual registry (ctx.residuals[:Rp] for the active balance \(R_{p,j}[t]\), and :Rq for reactive-capable formulations), indexed by bus and hour. Devices write their injections into the same registry; the assembly then closes each residual into a nodal-balance constraint — the constraint whose dual is \(\lambda_j[t]\). Nothing anywhere branches on if formulation == ...; even "does this model have reactive power?" is answered by whether :Rq exists in the registry, not by a flag. The concrete formulations — DCPowerFlow, LinDistFlow, ConvexBranchFlow (the SOCP with the exactness copy), ACPowerFlow (the nonconvex Ipopt oracle), RestrictedBranchFlow (overvoltage-capable OPF-m), MeshedFlow — all plug into the same slot. A conformance test proves the point mechanically: the same device vector and the same solve call, invoked once with DC and once with LinDistFlow, differ textually in the pf argument alone and yield the same price on a loss-less fixture.

2. The device seam: AbstractDevice

Prosumer devices (Thermostatic, Deferrable, Interruptible, PVBattery, and the later FourQuadBESS) each contribute their own variables, dynamics, and concave utility, and are rolled up by an Aggregator into the nodal net power \(p_{ag_j}[t]\) that enters the balance residual. Devices are unaware of which power-flow formulation is active, and vice versa — both meet only at the residual registry.

3. The solver seam: select_optimizer(::ProblemClass)

Exactly one file in the framework names concrete solvers. Models declare a problem class and ask the factory: 

model = Model(select_optimizer(SOCP()))   # never Model(Clarabel.Optimizer)

# Open-source defaults:
#   LP / MILP -> HiGHS
#   QP / SOCP -> Clarabel   (interior-point: accurate duals, i.e. accurate prices)
#   NLP       -> Ipopt      (the AC oracle)

Dispatch is by singleton type — no if class == chain — so the commercial fallbacks (Gurobi, Mosek) live in weak-dependency package extensions that extend the factory without ever becoming hard dependencies. The choice of Clarabel for the conic classes is load-bearing: the framework's product is duals, and an interior-point method's dual accuracy is what makes \(\lambda_j[t]\) a price you can publish rather than first-order-solver noise.

4. The strategy seam: how a scenario gets solved

The same materialized problem can be solved centrally (solve_welfare, one monolithic SOCP, duals read directly) or distributedly (solve_admm, the AGR-OPT/DSO-OPT dual-ascent loop with penalty \(\rho\)) — selected by one field of a declarative Scenario, with both paths normalized into an identical result schema so they are directly comparable. The research extensions that change the shape of a run rather than just the solve — rolling-horizon MPC and stochastic extensive-form — are deliberately separate entry points (run_mpc, run_stochastic) rather than more strategy branches, so the validated day-ahead dispatch path stays byte-identical.

The assembly point tells the whole story

The top module src/TSODSO.jl exports nothing and contains no logic — it is purely the include graph of the seams, in dependency order, with a comment per file recording which plan owns it and why it loads where it does. Reading it top to bottom is reading the architecture: units and data, solver factory, model context and status gate, the power-flow formulations, devices and the aggregator, the welfare solve and exactness gates, the oracle and certificates, pricing, ADMM, planning, diagnostics, and finally the experiment harness — orchestration layers always after the validated builders they orchestrate. Each seam file declares its own exports, so filling a seam never touches the assembly file.

Tech stack in one paragraph

The framework is pure Julia on JuMP (chosen over DCP-style modeling precisely because the product is the dual of a named constraint, and because ADMM/Benders outer loops demand parameterized re-solves of models built once — JuMP Parameters and RHS updates, never a rebuild inside a loop). Solvers are open-source-first behind the factory: Clarabel for QP/SOCP (accurate interior-point duals for price recovery), HiGHS for LP/MILP (Benders masters), Ipopt for the nonconvex AC oracle; Gurobi/Mosek only as weakdep-gated fallbacks. Reproducibility rides on DrWatson (seeded scenarios, provenance-stamped storage with the git commit, pinned Manifest.toml), documentation on Documenter + Literate (every model page executes its real solves at build time), figures on CairoMakie, and the ~2,800-test suite combines unit tests, pinned "gate-then-golden" regressions, certification cases, and Aqua/JET quality checks.

Where it lives: the include-order narrative is src/TSODSO.jl; the seams are src/powerflow/AbstractPowerFlow.jl (+ the formulations beside it), src/devices/, src/solver/factory.jl with src/solver/ProblemClass.jl, and src/experiments/run.jl for strategy dispatch; the repository map is in README.md.
See it run: "Rung 0: Toy DC" — the smallest page that exercises the full spine (factory, context, status gate, dual read) — and then any higher rung of the ladder.

The Network Model: Exact DistFlow, LinDistFlow, and a Certified SOCP Relaxation

This section is the mathematical heart of the framework. Everything downstream — the welfare objective, the ADMM decomposition, and above all the prices (which are constraint duals) — stands on the network model derived here. The chain is: exact nonconvex DistFlow → drop losses (LinDistFlow) → relax the one nonconvex equality to a second-order cone (SOCP) → certify, after every solve, that the relaxation closed tight. The last step is the framework's distinctive move: exactness is treated as an a-posteriori numerical certificate, not an a-priori theorem.

1. Setting: a radial feeder, and why distribution needs more than DC

Standing assumption (stated loudly): the entire operational layer models the distribution feeder as a balanced, positive-sequence, single-phase equivalent. Real distribution feeders are unbalanced and three-phase; this framework deliberately works with the balanced single-phase reduction (as the thesis does), and real three-phase data enters only after a positive-sequence reduction (Section 7). The network is radial: a tree rooted at the TSO–DSO frontier bus \(j = 0\), with branches \((i,j)\) oriented parent \(i\) → child \(j\). The Feeder constructor enforces radiality (\(|\mathcal{B}| = |\mathcal{N}| - 1\), assert_radial) — an invalid feeder cannot be constructed. All quantities are per-unit, converted from SI exactly once at ingestion.

Why does distribution need voltage and losses modeled at all? Transmission-style DC-OPF gets away with three assumptions: voltage magnitudes ≈ 1 pu everywhere, negligible resistance (\(r \ll x\)), and small angle differences. On a distribution feeder all three fail:

  • Voltage moves. Feeders run at 4–13 kV over resistive conductors; the voltage drop from root to leaf (or the voltage rise under PV back-feed) is exactly the quantity the operational constraints \(V_{\min} \le |V_j| \le V_{\max}\) police. A model with no voltage variable cannot see the binding constraint that, in the thesis's IEEE-123 case, drives the entire price signal.
  • Resistance dominates. Distribution \(r/x\) ratios are near or above 1, so real-power losses \(r_{ij}\ell_{ij}\) are first-order, not a correction.
  • Prices need physics. The DADP price at bus \(j\) is the dual of that bus's active balance. If the balance omits losses and voltage coupling, the dual decomposes into nothing — no loss component, no voltage component, no congestion component.

The framework makes this contrast concrete with its abstraction ladder. Rung 0 (docs/literate/toy_dc.jl) is a single-bus, single-period "DC" toy: nodal balance \(p_{\text{import}} - p_{\text{load}} = 0\), a linear welfare objective, and the balance's dual as the price. It exists to prove the pipeline (residual seams, solver factory, dual extraction) on a model with no network at all. Every rung above it swaps in a richer power-flow formulation through the same contribute! dispatch seam — device and assembly code never change.

Where it lives: src/powerflow/DCPowerFlow.jl, src/models/toy_dc.jl, src/core/ (the Feeder/Bus/Branch types and radiality check).
See it run: docs page "Rung 0 — The Toy DC Walking Skeleton" (docs/literate/toy_dc.jl).

2. The exact DistFlow (branch-flow) equations

The DistFlow model (Baran–Wu) describes steady-state power flow on a radial network using branch quantities instead of bus phasors. Fix a branch \((i,j)\) with series impedance \(z_{ij} = r_{ij} + \mathrm{i}\,x_{ij}\), sending-end (parent) voltage phasor \(V_i\), and branch current phasor \(I_{ij}\). Define the sending-end complex power \(S_{ij} = P_{ij} + \mathrm{i}\,Q_{ij} = V_i I_{ij}^*\). We derive every equation from Ohm's law plus this definition. (Time index \(t\) suppressed for clarity; every equation holds per hour \(t = 1,\dots,T\).)

  1. Square the power definition → the coupling identity. Take squared magnitudes of \(S_{ij} = V_i I_{ij}^*\): \[ |S_{ij}|^2 = |V_i|^2\,|I_{ij}|^2 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P_{ij}^2 + Q_{ij}^2 = v_i\,\ell_{ij}, \] where \(v_i = |V_i|^2\) and \(\ell_{ij} = |I_{ij}|^2\) are the squared voltage and current. This is not a modeling choice — it is an identity forced by the definitions. Written as a constraint on the squared variables: \[ \ell_{ij}[t]\, v_i[t] \;=\; P_{ij}[t]^2 + Q_{ij}[t]^2 . \tag{3.34} \] Physical reading: the current on a wire is determined by the power it carries and the voltage it carries it at. This single quadratic equality is the model's only nonconvexity — everything that follows in Sections 4–6 is about taming it.

  2. Power balance at the receiving end → nodal balances with a loss term. The power arriving at child bus \(j\) is what was sent minus what the wire dissipated: \(S_{ij} - z_{ij}|I_{ij}|^2\) (the series impedance carries current \(I_{ij}\), so it absorbs \(z_{ij}\ell_{ij}\)). Conservation at bus \(j\) — arrivals feed the local net injection \(p_j, q_j\) (in this framework, the aggregator's net consumption \(p_{ag_j}, q_{ag_j}\)) plus all outgoing child branches — gives the real part \[ P_{ij}[t] - r_{ij}\,\ell_{ij}[t] \;-\; p_j[t] \;-\; \sum_{m\,:\,j \to m} P_{jm}[t] \;=\; 0 \tag{3.31} \] and the imaginary part \[ Q_{ij}[t] - x_{ij}\,\ell_{ij}[t] \;-\; q_j[t] \;-\; \sum_{m\,:\,j \to m} Q_{jm}[t] \;=\; 0 . \tag{3.32} \] Physical reading: \(r_{ij}\ell_{ij}\) is the \(I^2 r\) heating loss of the conductor; \(x_{ij}\ell_{ij}\) is the reactive power absorbed by its series reactance. Note the code's convention (a deliberate, documented choice): losses are charged at the child node — the incoming branch contributes \(+P - r\ell\) to the child's balance, outgoing branches contribute \(-P\). The dual of (3.31) at bus \(j\) is the DADP price \(\lambda_j[t]\) — the reason this equation, of all of them, gets a named residual (:Rp).

  3. Ohm's law across the branch → the voltage-drop equation. Kirchhoff's voltage law gives \(V_j = V_i - z_{ij} I_{ij}\). Square it: \[ |V_j|^2 = |V_i|^2 - 2\,\mathrm{Re}\!\left(V_i \,(z_{ij} I_{ij})^*\right) + |z_{ij}|^2 |I_{ij}|^2 . \] For the cross term, use \(V_i I_{ij}^* = S_{ij}\): \(\mathrm{Re}(V_i z_{ij}^* I_{ij}^*) = \mathrm{Re}(z_{ij}^* S_{ij}) = r_{ij}P_{ij} + x_{ij}Q_{ij}\). Hence \[ v_j[t] \;=\; v_i[t] \;-\; 2\left(r_{ij}P_{ij}[t] + x_{ij}Q_{ij}[t]\right) \;+\; \left(r_{ij}^2 + x_{ij}^2\right)\ell_{ij}[t] . \tag{3.33} \] Physical reading: the middle term is the familiar first-order voltage drop driven by the power flowing toward the load (or the voltage rise when \(P_{ij} < 0\), i.e. PV back-feed); the last term is the second-order correction from the loss current itself. The magic of the squared-variable formulation: phase angles have been eliminated exactly — on a radial network, (3.31)–(3.34) with squared variables are equivalent to the full AC power-flow equations, with the angles recoverable afterwards.

  4. Operating limits. Voltage magnitude bounds become bounds on the squared variable (a classic off-by-square pitfall the code guards loudly — the bounds are \(V_{\min}^2, V_{\max}^2\), and the root is fixed at \(v_0 = 1.0 = 1.0^2\)): \[ V_{\min}^2 \;\le\; v_j[t] \;\le\; V_{\max}^2 , \tag{3.35} \] and branch thermal (apparent-power) limits: \[ P_{ij}[t]^2 + Q_{ij}[t]^2 \;\le\; S_{\max,ij}^2 . \tag{3.36} \] Code note: the implementation adds the cone (3.36) only on branches with a genuine limit (the thesis's cases constrain only the head branch); interior branches carry a documented no-limit sentinel (SMAX_NO_LIMIT) and get no cone, so cases stay congestion-driven at the head rather than over-constrained by fictitious interior limits. The thesis's separate reverse-direction limit (3.37) is not implemented as a second constraint — (3.36) already bounds \(P^2 + Q^2\) symmetrically in sign.

Summary. The exact branch-flow model is (3.31)–(3.36): all constraints are linear in \((P, Q, v, \ell)\) except the single quadratic equality (3.34). An optimization over this feasible set is nonconvex — solvers can only promise local optima, and the duals of a local solution carry no global price meaning. That is unacceptable for a framework whose entire product is duals-as-prices.

Where it lives: the exact (equality) form is implemented as the nonconvex oracle src/powerflow/ACPowerFlow.jl (Section 5); the relaxed form in src/powerflow/ConvexBranchFlow.jl, whose comments trace every constraint to these equation numbers.

3. LinDistFlow: the loss-less linear rung

Before relaxing (3.34), it pays to ask what happens if we simply delete \(\ell\). Setting \(\ell_{ij} \to 0\) in (3.31)–(3.33) drops the loss terms \(r\ell,\ x\ell\) from the balances and the quadratic correction \((r^2+x^2)\ell\) from the voltage drop, leaving the LinDistFlow model: linear balances plus the linear voltage-drop relation

\[ v_j[t] \;=\; v_i[t] \;-\; 2\left(r_{ij}P_{ij}[t] + x_{ij}Q_{ij}[t]\right) . \tag{3.43\(\vert_{\ell\to 0}\)} \]

(The code tags this equation 3.43 because it is the \(\ell \to 0\) specialization of the thesis's exactness-copy recursion — see Section 5; in the thesis's own numbering the underlying relation is (3.33) with the current term dropped.)

When is it a good approximation? When losses are small relative to the flows (\(r_{ij}\ell_{ij} \ll |P_{ij}|\)) and voltages stay near nominal — the standard lightly-loaded distribution regime. Errors grow with loading squared, since \(\ell \sim (P^2+Q^2)/v\).

Its two roles in this framework:

  1. A cheap rung. As a pure LP/QP formulation it solves with HiGHS/Clarabel at trivial cost, exercises the full residual-seam machinery (including the reactive channel :Rq that Rung 0 lacked), and already yields a meaningful nodal dual. It is the natural first multi-bus model for a new scenario.
  2. The exactness "copy" trick. The same linear voltage recursion, instantiated a second time as auxiliary variables \(\hat v_j\) alongside the true SOCP model, is the thesis's device (3.43)–(3.45) for steering the SOC relaxation to exactness. LinDistFlow is thus not discarded when the SOCP arrives — it rides along inside it.

Where it lives: src/powerflow/LinDistFlow.jl, src/models/linear_solve.jl.
See it run: docs page "Rung 1-2 — LinDistFlow" (docs/literate/lindistflow.jl).

4. The SOCP relaxation

The convexification move is minimal and surgical: keep every linear constraint of Section 2 unchanged, and relax the single nonconvex equality (3.34) to an inequality:

\[ \ell_{ij}[t]\, v_i[t] \;\ge\; P_{ij}[t]^2 + Q_{ij}[t]^2 . \tag{3.39} \]

Geometric reading: (3.34) is the boundary surface of the set defined by (3.39). Relaxing equality to "≥" fills in everything above the surface — and that filled set is convex. Concretely, (3.39) says the squared current is allowed to be an over-estimate of the physical current. Points strictly inside the cone correspond to a fictitious extra current (hence fictitious extra losses \(r\ell\)) that no physical operating point produces.

Why (3.39) is a rotated second-order cone

The rotated second-order cone in \(\mathbb{R}^{n+2}\) is the set \(\{(u_1, u_2, w) : \|w\|_2^2 \le 2 u_1 u_2,\ u_1, u_2 \ge 0\}\). Choose \(u_1 = \tfrac{1}{2}\ell_{ij}\), \(u_2 = v_i\), \(w = (P_{ij}, Q_{ij})\):

\[ P_{ij}^2 + Q_{ij}^2 \;\le\; 2\cdot\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\ell_{ij}\right)\cdot v_i \;=\; \ell_{ij}\,v_i , \]

which is exactly (3.39), with the required nonnegativity supplied by \(\ell_{ij} \ge 0\) (explicit variable bound) and \(v_i \ge V_{\min}^2 > 0\). In JuMP, verbatim from ConvexBranchFlow.jl:

@constraint(m, cone[b = 1:nB, t = 1:T],
    [0.5 * l[b, t], v[B[b].from, t], P[b, t], Q[b, t]] in RotatedSecondOrderCone())

The 0.5 factor is mandatory — JuMP's cone enforces \(\|w\|^2 \le 2u_1u_2\), so omitting it silently doubles the allowed current, a bug the repo's research notes flag as a named anti-pattern. The thermal limit (3.36) is likewise a (plain) second-order cone: [smax, P, Q] in SecondOrderCone() ⟺ \(P^2+Q^2 \le S_{\max}^2\).

Why relax at all?

Because convexity buys the two things this framework cannot live without:

  • A global optimum. The welfare problem over the relaxed set is an SOCP — interior-point solvers (Clarabel) find the optimum with a certificate, reproducibly. No local-solution ambiguity.
  • Meaningful duals. A convex program satisfying Slater's condition has strong duality: the multiplier \(\lambda_j[t]\) on the nodal balance (3.31) is a true shadow price — the marginal social-welfare value of one more unit of power at bus \(j\), hour \(t\). This dual is the DADP, the dynamic distribution price the whole transactive scheme is built on (the pricing section of this guide). On the nonconvex exact model, no such interpretation survives. The registered cone/voltage/thermal duals additionally decompose the DADP into energy + loss + voltage + congestion components (the DLMP decomposition).

The price of the relaxation is the obvious one: the optimizer may exploit the fictitious region strictly inside the cone. Whether it did is the exactness question.

Where it lives: src/powerflow/ConvexBranchFlow.jl (cone, both voltage drops, loss terms, thermal cones, and the dual registrations for the DLMP split); src/models/welfare_solve.jl (the GLB-CVX assembly solve_welfare).
See it run: docs page "Rung 3 — SOCP Convex Branch-Flow & the LinDistFlow Exactness Copy" (docs/literate/convex_branch_flow.jl).

5. Exactness: a steering trick plus a refusal gate, not a theorem

The relaxation is called exact at a solved point when (3.39) holds with equality on every branch and hour — i.e. the relaxed optimum happens to lie on the physical surface (3.34), so it is an exact AC solution and the duals are physically meaningful prices. Classical theory (Farivar & Low 2013; Gan, Li, Topcu & Low 2015) proves exactness for radial networks under conditions — essentially, that the upper voltage bound does not strictly bind — and identifies the over-voltage / reverse-flow regime of a high-PV feeder as precisely where it can fail. The framework's operational posture is therefore layered:

5.1 The LinDistFlow exactness copy (3.43–3.45): steering the optimum toward the surface

Following the thesis, the model carries an auxiliary squared voltage \(\hat v_j\) — the "copy" — obeying the LinDistFlow-style recursion evaluated on loss-adjusted flows \(\hat P = P + r\ell\), \(\hat Q = Q + x\ell\):

\[ \hat v_j[t] \;=\; \hat v_i[t] \;-\; 2\Bigl\{\, r_{ij}\bigl(P_{ij}[t] + r_{ij}\ell_{ij}[t]\bigr) + x_{ij}\bigl(Q_{ij}[t] + x_{ij}\ell_{ij}[t]\bigr) \Bigr\} , \tag{3.43} \]

and both voltages are held in the same physical band:

\[ V_{\min}^2 \;\le\; v_j[t],\ \hat v_j[t] \;\le\; V_{\max}^2 . \tag{3.45} \]

Why this is not decorative. Expand the \(\ell\)-dependence of the two recursions: the true drop (3.33) carries \(+(r^2+x^2)\,\ell\), while the copy drop (3.43) carries \(-2(r^2+x^2)\,\ell\) — opposite responses to the same loss current. A solution that inflates a fictitious \(\ell\) pushes \(v\) and \(\hat v\) apart; forcing both to live inside the same band (3.45) removes the room the relaxation would otherwise have to exploit, pressing \(\ell\) down until the cone (3.39) closes with equality. In the exact limit \(\ell \to 0\) both recursions collapse to the same LinDistFlow relation of Section 3 — the geometric face of exactness is the two voltage profiles coinciding. Two implementation notes where the code sharpens the thesis: the copy is written purely in the original \(P, Q, \ell\) plus the single new variable \(\hat v\) (no separate \(\hat P, \hat Q\) flow network is instantiated), and the copy's root is fixed to the same reference \(\hat v_0 = 1.0\).

Honesty requires the next sentence: the thesis presents the copy as guaranteeing equality at the optimum. The repo's own experiments (Section 6) show that claim has boundaries — so the copy is treated as a steering device, and whether the cone actually closed is checked, every time, by the gate below.

5.2 The certificate: assert_socp_exact!, the price-refusal gate

After every trusted solve (status check passed, before any dual() is read), solve_welfare computes the per-branch, per-hour relaxation gap

\[ \mathrm{gap}[b,t] \;=\; \bigl|\, \ell_{b}[t]\, v_{i(b)}[t] \;-\; \bigl(P_{b}[t]^2 + Q_{b}[t]^2\bigr) \bigr| \]

and requires, per branch (an isapprox-style, scale-free combined bound; defaults \(r_{\text{tol}} = 10^{-4}\), \(a_{\text{tol}} = 10^{-6}\)):

\[ \mathrm{gap}[b,t] \;\le\; a_{\text{tol}} \;+\; r_{\text{tol}}\cdot \max\bigl(|\ell v|,\ |P^2+Q^2|\bigr) . \]

The relative term makes the verdict invariant to the per-unit base (the gap is in pu², so a purely absolute tolerance would judge the same physical slack differently on a 1 MVA vs 100 MVA base); the absolute floor keeps near-zero-flow branches from tripping on rounding noise. On violation the gate throws, refusing to return any price: a strict cone means \(\ell\) is a fictitious over-current and the DADP duals are meaningless — and crucially, the solver reports OPTIMAL either way; without this gate there is no error to warn you. On success the worst absolute gap is reported as a first-class output (ctx.meta[:socp_maxgap], ~\(10^{-8}\) on benign radial feeders).

5.3 Ground truth: the nonconvex AC oracle

A certificate computed from the relaxed model's own solution answers "did the cone close?" but not "is the closed solution the true AC optimum?" For that the framework keeps a genuinely independent oracle: ACPowerFlow enforces (3.34) as a true equality \(\ell v = P^2 + Q^2\) and solves the resulting nonconvex NLP with Ipopt (multi-start validated against a closed-form 2-bus phasor). assert_ac_exact! compares the SOCP and AC solutions built from identical data, hour by hour — and, by design, it never throws: a relaxation gap against ground truth is a finding to report, not a defect to refuse. Re-solving the same cone through a different conic solver could never detect inexactness (same relaxed feasible set); only an independent nonconvex formulation can.

Radial-required caveat. Every exactness statement above is for radial networks — the setting of the Farivar–Low / Gan–Low results and of the thesis. The squared-variable model drops phase angles, which is only innocuous on a tree; on a meshed network angle consistency around loops becomes a real constraint, and the repo handles that regime in a separate rung with an explicit angle-recovery certificate (src/powerflow/MeshedFlow.jl, src/models/mesh_angle_certificate.jl) rather than by silently reusing the radial machinery.

Where it lives: src/models/exactness.jl (assert_socp_exact!), src/powerflow/ACPowerFlow.jl and src/models/ac_oracle.jl (assert_ac_exact!).
See it run: docs pages "Rung 3 — SOCP Convex Branch-Flow" and "Rung 3 — AC-Exactness Oracle" (docs/literate/convex_branch_flow.jl, docs/literate/ac_oracle.jl).

6. When exactness fails — the honest part

The repo does not merely warn that inexactness is possible; it manufactures it, reproduces it, and maps its boundary. This is the v2.1 milestone's headline scientific finding.

The failure mechanism, observed live. On a 3-bus stress fixture (low-impedance branches \(r = x = 0.05\), tight voltage band) with PV scaled to 1.2× — the over-voltage, reverse-flow regime — the SOCP pins a bus voltage at the squared upper bound \(V_{\max}^2 = 1.05^2 = 1.1025\) while carrying reverse (back-feed) flow, and inflates the fictitious current: the internal gap socp_maxgap jumps from the benign feeder's ~\(10^{-8}\) to order 10 — a genuine, structural relaxation gap, confirmed by the independent AC oracle flagging a run of inexact afternoon hours. This is exactly the boundary Farivar–Low and Gan–Low predict, hit numerically. Under the default gate those prices are refused; the literate pages deliberately override the gate (rtol_exact) to expose the loose solution for study. The boundary is also a knife-edge: the milestone found the exact↔inexact transition non-monotonic near the boundary, with small population-scale perturbations (±2–5%) flipping the classification — which is why price results in that regime are reported as directional, not magnitude-exact.

Mapping the applicability region. Since the detector is free (the certificate is computed from the SOCP solution it already has — no oracle needed), the repo sweeps the (PV scale, load scale, \(V_{\max}\)) space and classifies every point exact / inexact / infeasible / guard-tripped, alongside two free diagnostics the classical theory says matter: is the upper voltage bound active, and does reverse flow occur.

The two maps together carry the methodological lesson the repo insists on: on the synthetic fixture the failure is structural (the gap persists as solver tolerances tighten, ratios \(10^3\)–\(10^4\)); on real IEEE-123 impedances the flagged points are interior-point convergence artifacts (ratios ~1–5 that collapse ~1000× when tol_gap tightens from \(10^{-8}\) to \(10^{-10}\)), and reverse flow alone — present at every solved point — predicts nothing. A tolerance ladder, not a single threshold, separates physics from numerics; and boundary values measured on one feeder do not transfer to another.

The constructive answer: an overvoltage-capable restriction. When a scenario must operate in the failing regime, the framework does not loosen the gate — it tightens the feasible set. RestrictedBranchFlow implements Gan–Low's "modified OPF" (OPF-m) construction: their Theorem 1 conditions are C1 (checkable a priori from impedances and bounds alone) and C2 (the optimal injections must land where the loss-free shadow voltage \(\hat v_{GL}\) stays under \(V_{\max}^2\) — not checkable a priori, and exactly what fails above). Adding the constraint \(\hat v_{GL} \le V_{\max}^2\) forces C2 by construction; since Lemma 1 gives \(v \le \hat v_{GL}\) unconditionally, this is a genuine restriction (a subset of the physical feasible set) whose SOC relaxation is provably exact — trading a slice of feasible operating room for trustworthy prices in the overvoltage regime.

Where it lives: src/powerflow/RestrictedBranchFlow.jl, src/models/restriction_exactness.jl, scripts/socp_applicability_sweep.jl (map generator; results committed under results/socp_applicability/).
See it run: docs pages "SOC Relaxation Applicability" (docs/literate/socp_applicability.jl) and "Rung 3 — Overvoltage-Capable Relaxation" (docs/literate/restricted_branch_flow.jl).

7. Real network data: IEEE-13 / IEEE-123 fixtures

The models above run on two feeder families: the modified IEEE-13 (the thesis's congestion-driven Case A) and the modified IEEE-123 (the voltage-constrained Case B, 4.16 kV, 85 load nodes). Since the thesis's own impedance appendix is not publicly redistributable, the IEEE-123 fixture's branch impedances come from public OpenDSS test-case data via a documented reduction recipe:

  1. Fetch the official IEEE 123-bus OpenDSS files (master + line codes; vendored under scripts/data/ for offline reproducibility).
  2. Reduce each 3×3 (or 2×2) phase-impedance matrix to positive sequence by the Fortescue-averaging identity — consistent with the balanced single-phase-equivalent assumption of Section 1: \[ R_1 = \operatorname{mean}(\text{diag}) - \operatorname{mean}(\text{offdiag}), \qquad\text{(same for } X_1\text{)}, \] with the \(1\times 1\) single-phase-lateral short-circuit \(R_1 = r_{11}\). This assumes approximately transposed, balanced construction — an approximation, stated as such.
  3. Convert Ω → per-unit exactly once, at ingestion (\(z_\Omega = R_1 \times \text{Length}\), no unit scale factor — the OpenDSS files leave Units= implicit, and applying a feet/miles/kft factor here would corrupt every impedance by orders of magnitude).

Caveats carried honestly: regulators, capacitors, and switches are collapsed into near-ideal synthetic switch impedances rather than actively modeled; only the 117 ordinary branches carry real per-segment data. It is these real, much-lower impedances that produce Section 6's finding that the overvoltage inexactness mechanism cannot fire on IEEE-123 in the swept region.

Where it lives: src/data/ieee123.jl, src/data/ieee123_impedances.jl (committed reduction output), scripts/reduce_ieee123_impedances.jl (generator with pinned --verify self-checks).
See it run: docs page "IEEE-123 Real Impedances — Public-Data Reduction" (docs/literate/ieee123_impedances.jl).

Prosumers, Devices, and Aggregators

The previous section built the wires. This section builds the people on the wires: households that own air conditioners, washing machines, rooftop PV, and batteries, and that respond to prices. Everything the market section (next) does — welfare maximization, prices as duals — rests on the device models here, because in this framework flexibility is never postulated as an abstract "demand elasticity"; it emerges from device physics. An A/C can shift consumption only as far as the thermal mass of the house allows; a washer can defer only inside its window; a battery can arbitrage only what its state of charge and efficiency permit. The optimization discovers the flexibility that the physical constraints leave open.

The prosumer's problem

A prosumer household derives utility from consuming energy services (a cool room, a finished wash cycle, a charged battery) and pays a price for the energy behind them. In isolation, its problem at bus \(j\) over hours \(t = 1,\dots,T\) is

\[ \max_{x \in \mathcal{X}_{\text{device}}} \; U(x) \;+\; \sum_t \lambda_j[t]\, p_j[t](x), \]

where \(x\) collects all device decision variables, \(\mathcal{X}_{\text{device}}\) is the intersection of every device's physical constraint set, \(p_j[t]\) is the household's signed net injection at its bus (negative when consuming — the framework's uniform sign convention), and \(\lambda_j[t]\) is the nodal price it faces. A positive injection (PV export, battery discharge) earns \(\lambda_j\); consumption pays it. Two modeling commitments make this problem well-behaved:

  • Every utility is concave quadratic (thesis eqs. 3.10–3.20), with strictly positive curvature enforced by constructor guards (b > 0, thrown as ArgumentError otherwise). Concavity is what keeps the assembled social-welfare problem a convex QP whose duals — the prices — are trustworthy.
  • Every constraint set is affine (linear recursions, bounds, budget bands), with no binaries anywhere. Even the battery, which naively wants a charge-XOR-discharge binary, gets away without one (see below). A single integer variable would destroy the duals the whole pricing scheme is built on.

The framework implements three prosumer device types (plus an Interruptible elastic load from an earlier rung and a FourQuadBESS reactive-capable storage for the meshed extension, both out of scope here). Each is an immutable Julia struct whose constructor validates physics up front, and each contributes to a shared JuMP model through one seam, contribute!.

Thermostatic load — thermal RC dynamics and a comfort band

Motivation and derivation

An air conditioner is flexible because a house stores heat. Model the house as a first-order thermal RC circuit (the "equivalent thermal parameter" / ETP model): indoor temperature \(T_{in}\) relaxes toward ambient \(T_{out}\) through a thermal resistance, while the A/C pumps heat out in proportion to its electrical draw \(p\). Newton's cooling law, \(C\,\dot T_{in} = (T_{out} - T_{in})/R - \kappa\, p\), discretized with step \(\Delta t\) and writing \(\alpha = \Delta t/(RC)\), \(\beta = \kappa \Delta t / C\), gives the linear recursion the code implements verbatim:

\[ T_{in}[t+1] \;=\; T_{in}[t] \;+\; \alpha\,\bigl(T_{out}[t] - T_{in}[t]\bigr) \;-\; \beta\, p[t] \tag{3.2} \] \[ T_{min} \;\le\; T_{in}[t] \;\le\; T_{max} \tag{3.3} \]

with power bounds \(P_{min} \le p[t] \le P_{max}\). The constructor rejects \(\alpha < 0\) (heat flowing from cold to hot — a second-law violation) and \(\beta \le 0\) (power that fails to cool — a silent sign flip that would invert the whole model), and requires the initial condition \(T_{min} \le T_{in}[1] = T_{in0} \le T_{max}\) so the band constraint cannot make the first step cryptically infeasible.

Utility

Comfort is a concave quadratic penalty on deviation from the bottom of the band (thesis eq. 3.11; the additive constant \(c\) is dropped since it never affects the argmax):

\[ U(T_{in}) \;=\; -\frac{b}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl(T_{in}[t] - T_{min}\bigr)^{2} \tag{3.11} \]

Interpretation. This is an A/C model in a cooling climate: the household would ideally hold \(T_{in} = T_{min}\) (maximally cool), and \(b\) prices how much it minds being warmer. Note this differs from the naive textbook "penalize distance from a mid-band setpoint": the utility pulls toward \(T_{min}\), and the price is what pushes back. At a high nodal price the optimizer lets \(T_{in}\) ride up toward \(T_{max}\) (pre-cooling in cheap hours, then coasting) — flexibility emerging from the thermal mass encoded in \(\alpha, \beta\), exactly as promised.

Deferrable load — an energy budget inside a window

Constraints

A shiftable task (washer, EV charge) needs a certain amount of energy inside a contiguous window \([t_{start}, t_{end}]\) and draws nothing outside it:

\[ E_{min} \;\le\; \sum_{t \in [t_{start},\, t_{end}]} p[t] \;\le\; E , \qquad 0 \le p[t] \le P_{max} \;\; (t \text{ in window}), \quad p[t] = 0 \text{ otherwise} \tag{3.4–3.5} \]

Outside the window the variable's bounds are simply pinned to zero — no extra constraint rows. The constructor rejects infeasible budgets up front (\(E > P_{max}\cdot(t_{end}-t_{start}+1)\), or \(E_{min} \notin [0, E]\)), turning what would be a cryptic solver infeasibility into a clear ArgumentError.

Utility — and a deliberate departure from the naive formulation

\[ U(p) \;=\; -\frac{b}{2}\Bigl(\sum_{t\in\text{window}} p[t] \;-\; E\Bigr)^{2} \tag{3.12} \]

The naive version makes \(\sum p = E\) a hard equality — but then \(U \equiv 0\) on the feasible set and the curvature \(b\) is a dead parameter. The code instead makes the upper budget an inequality (\(\sum p \le E\)), so (3.12) is a live soft target: utility peaks when the task completes its full budget \(E\), and \(b\) genuinely trades completing the task against the price of the energy. The floor \(E_{min}\) (added as a constraint only when positive) is the must-complete knob: \(E_{min}=0\) is a purely elastic task that may skip entirely when energy is dear; \(E_{min}>0\) is an EV that must reach some charge, trading only the slack \([E_{min}, E]\) against price. The utility depends only on the window total — a deferrable task is indifferent to when it runs inside its window, which is precisely what makes it a shifting resource.

PV + battery — SOC dynamics and the no-binary trick

Constraints

A co-located rooftop PV array and battery schedules continuous charge \(p_{ch}[t]\ge 0\), discharge \(p_{dch}[t]\ge 0\), state of charge \(soc[t]\), and — a code addition beyond the thesis text — a curtailment variable \(pv_{used}[t]\):

\[ soc[t+1] \;=\; soc[t] \;+\; \Bigl(\eta\, p_{ch}[t] \;-\; \frac{p_{dch}[t]}{\eta}\Bigr)\Delta t \tag{3.6} \] \[ 0 \le p_{ch}[t] \le pv_{used}[t] \le P_{pv}[t] \tag{3.7} \] \[ 0 \le p_{ch}[t],\, p_{dch}[t] \le P_{max}, \qquad E_{min} \le soc[t] \le E_{max}, \quad soc[1] = soc_0 \tag{3.8–3.9} \]

Three honest assumptions baked in: the battery charges from PV only, never the grid (thesis Assumption A6 — eq. 3.7 bounds the charge by the used PV); PV and battery are active-power-only devices (Assumption A3 — they contribute no reactive term); and PV is curtailable (\(pv_{used} \le P_{pv}\)), a code refinement without which a high-PV hour with nowhere to put the surplus would be flat-out infeasible. The round-trip efficiency enters asymmetrically — \(\eta\) on the way in, \(1/\eta\) on the way out — so a full cycle returns only \(\eta^2 < 1\) of the energy. That loss is not a nuisance; it is half of the correctness argument below.

Utility — the Appendix C parametrization

The battery's preference is a concave charge utility minus a convex discharge cost, with all four coefficients derived from a single price triple \(\lambda_{min} < \lambda_{med} < \lambda_{max}\) (\(\lambda_{med}\) is the owner's indifference price):

\[ U_{batt} \;=\; \sum_t \Bigl[\, a_{ch}\, p_{ch}[t] - \tfrac{b_{ch}}{2} p_{ch}[t]^2 \;-\; a_{dch}\, p_{dch}[t] - \tfrac{b_{dch}}{2} p_{dch}[t]^2 \Bigr] \tag{3.15–3.16} \] \[ a_{ch} = a_{dch} = \lambda_{med}, \qquad b_{ch} = \frac{\lambda_{med}-\lambda_{min}}{P_{max}}, \qquad b_{dch} = \frac{\lambda_{max}-\lambda_{med}}{P_{max}} \tag{3.17–3.20} \]

Why no binary is needed (App. C, pp. 166–168)

A textbook battery model adds a binary or a complementarity constraint \(p_{ch}\cdot p_{dch} = 0\) to forbid simultaneous charge and discharge. Either would destroy the convexity — and with it the duals that are this framework's product. The code adds neither. Instead, observe the marginals:

\[ \frac{\partial U_{ch}}{\partial p_{ch}} = \lambda_{med} - b_{ch}\, p_{ch} \;\le\; \lambda_{med}, \qquad \frac{\partial C_{dch}}{\partial p_{dch}} = \lambda_{med} + b_{dch}\, p_{dch} \;\ge\; \lambda_{med}. \]

A simultaneous round-trip of \(\delta > 0\) through both legs gains at most \(\lambda_{med}\,\delta\) in charge utility, costs at least \(\lambda_{med}\,\delta\) in discharge cost — and with the strict ordering both curvatures are strictly positive, so for \(\delta > 0\) the utility change is strictly negative. Meanwhile the round-trip drains SOC by \((\,\eta - 1/\eta\,)\delta\,\Delta t < 0\). Simultaneous charge/discharge is therefore strictly dominated at any optimum: \(p_{ch}[t]\cdot p_{dch}[t] = 0\) holds automatically. The strictness of \(\lambda_{min} < \lambda_{med} < \lambda_{max}\) is load-bearing — a non-strict ordering zeroes a curvature, flattens the dominance to a tie, and admits SOC-draining co-optima — so the constructor throws on any non-strict triple, and solve_welfare verifies the product numerically after every solve (assert_battery_complementarity!: \(p_{ch}\cdot p_{dch} < \tau\, P_{max}^2\), a scale-free relative test). Correctness by parametrization, certified by measurement — never assumed.

The aggregator — rolling a bus's devices into one net injection

The network never sees individual devices. An Aggregator at bus \(j\) holds a set of member devices, a load power factor \(\varphi\), and an inelastic demand profile \(P_{dc}[t]\) (a parameter, not a decision — the fridge and lights run regardless). It rolls its members into the three nodal quantities of thesis eqs. 3.21–3.23:

\[ U_{ag} = \sum_d U_d \tag{3.21} \] \[ p_{ag}[t] = \sum_d p_{inject,d}[t] \;-\; P_{dc}[t] \tag{3.22} \] \[ q_{ag}[t] = -\,P_{dc}[t]\,\tan(\arccos\varphi) \tag{3.23} \]

Two honest notes on how the code relates to the thesis text. First, a sign convention flip: thesis (3.22) is written consumption-positive (\(p_{ag} > 0\) = net consumption), while the code uses injection-positive throughout (loads contribute \(-p\), PV/ discharge contribute \(+\)), so the code's \(p_{ag}\) is the thesis's negated. One convention, applied everywhere, checked by regression. Second, reactive power lives at the aggregator, not the devices: per Assumption A3 the DERs are active-only, so the only reactive draw is the inelastic load's, derived from its power factor via \(\tan(\arccos\varphi) = \sqrt{1-\varphi^2}/\varphi\) (single-sourced in reactive_factor). Devices with a genuine reactive decision (the meshed-grid FourQuadBESS) opt in through an optional q_inject field that the aggregator detects with a hasproperty check — existing devices needed zero changes when that contract was widened.

Why the aggregate stays convex (GLB-CVX)

Each member utility is a concave QuadExpr; a sum of concave functions is concave, so \(U_{ag}\) is concave (3.21). Each member's constraint set is affine, and (3.22)–(3.23) are affine maps of the member variables, so the aggregator's feasible set is a convex polyhedron and its net injection is affine in the decisions. Aggregation therefore preserves the convexity the devices were designed with — the assembled social-welfare problem stays a convex QP (or SOCP once the branch-flow cone joins), which is exactly what "GLB-CVX" names. No approximation, no convexification step: convexity is compositional by construction.

The contribute! composition seam

Every model element — power-flow formulation, device, aggregator — enters the shared JuMP model through one generic function, contribute!(thing, ctx; T), operating on a shared ModelContext (the JuMP model plus residual accumulators and registered-constraint handles). The device contract has two variants:

  • Aggregatable devices (Thermostatic, Deferrable, PVBattery) build only their own variables and constraints on ctx.model, then return a NamedTuple (; vars, p_inject, utility): their decision-variable container, their signed per-hour active injection (a Vector{AffExpr}, loads negative), and their concave utility (a QuadExpr — routed as a quadratic expression precisely so the curvature survives; pushing it through the affine residual would silently drop it). They touch neither the network residuals nor the objective.
  • The aggregator is the sole network-facing writer: it drives each member's contribute!, sums the returned pieces per (3.21)–(3.22), writes exactly one net active term into the nodal residual :Rp and one net reactive term into :Rq at its bus, adds the summed utility to the welfare objective via add_to_objective!, and stashes the device variables in ctx.meta[:agg_device_vars] for post-solve checks (the battery complementarity certificate, the figure below).

This is the decoupling that makes the framework a research bench: a device never sees the network object (it holds only a bus id and receives \(T\)), so swapping the power-flow formulation — DC, LinDistFlow, full SOCP branch flow — touches no device code, and adding a device touches no network code. Initial conditions and forecast profiles (\(T_{in0}\), \(soc_0\), \(P_{pv}\), \(P_{dc}\), \(T_{out}\)) are genuine JuMP Parameters, so the rolling-horizon (MPC) orchestrator re-targets them with set_parameter_value instead of rebuilding the model each step.

The figure is read directly off a solved model (the literate docs page executes the real solve_welfare at build time — the numbers cannot drift from the code). Three panels, one physical unit each:

  • Top — net injections (the summands of eq. 3.22). The gray dashed line is the fixed inelastic baseline \(-P_{dc}\); the black line is the aggregator net \(p_{ag}\) the network actually sees. The honest finding on this fixture: both flexible loads sit flat at zero — at \(\lambda_0 = 6\) the deferrable task (a live preference with \(E_{min}=0\)) finds backing off entirely cheaper than paying for its soft target, and the A/C likewise declines to draw. The flexibility story is carried by the battery, whose green injection \(pv_{used} - p_{ch} + p_{dch}\) discharges against the priced frontier. High price, devices back off, storage sells: the demand response the thesis promises, produced by device physics rather than an elasticity assumption.
  • Middle — thermostatic state (3.2–3.3). \(T_{in}\) rides the ambient \(T_{out}\) inside the shaded comfort band: the comfort utility (3.11) pulls it toward \(T_{min}\) exactly as hard as the price lets it — here, not at all.
  • Bottom — battery SOC (3.6, 3.9). The intertemporal state that couples the hours, drawing down between its dashed \(E_{min}/E_{max}\) bounds as the battery monetizes its stored energy.

The Market: Welfare Maximization and Prices as Duals

This is the centerpiece of the whole framework. The thesis's transactive scheme does not design a tariff and then check whether it works; it solves one convex social-welfare problem over the physical network and recovers the price at every bus and hour as the Lagrange multiplier of that bus's power balance. The day-ahead dynamic price (DADP) — a distribution-level locational marginal price (DLMP) — is a mathematical by-product of the optimum, and it comes with a theorem: a prosumer who selfishly optimizes against that price chooses exactly the schedule the social optimum wanted from it. Prices are never postulated, always recovered. This section derives that claim step by step, then dissects the price into its physical components, exactly as the code computes them.

Assembling the social-welfare problem (GLB-CVX)

Take the pieces from the previous two sections. The network section gave us the SOCP branch-flow feasible set on the radial feeder: squared voltages \(v_j\) and their exactness copy \(\hat v_j\), branch flows \(P_b, Q_b\), squared currents \(l_b \ge 0\), coupled by the voltage drops (3.33/3.43), the rotated cone \(l_b v_i \ge P_b^2 + Q_b^2\) (3.39), the apparent-power limits (3.36), and the voltage bounds (3.45). The devices section gave us each aggregator's concave utility \(U_{ag_j}\) and affine net injections \(p_{ag_j}[t], q_{ag_j}[t]\). One element remains: the frontier. At the root bus \(j = 0\) — the TSO–DSO boundary — the feeder exchanges power with the wholesale market (MEM) at the exogenous price \(\lambda_0[t]\), through a variable \(p_{import}[t]\) (free-sign when allow_export = true: positive buys, negative sells at the same \(\lambda_0\)).

The centralized problem the code assembles in solve_welfare is (thesis eq. 3.38):

\[ \max_{\substack{x_j \in \mathcal{X}_j,\; p_{import},\\ v, \hat v, P, Q, l}} \;\; \sum_{j} U_{ag_j}(x_j) \;-\; \sum_{t=1}^{T} \lambda_0[t]\, p_{import}[t] \tag{3.38} \]

subject to, at every bus \(j\) and hour \(t\), the nodal active-power balance (inflow minus losses, minus outflow, plus local net injection, plus the frontier exchange at the root — the residual \(R_{p,j}\) the code accumulates and then closes to zero):

\[ R_{p,j}[t] \;=\; \underbrace{P_{i j}[t] - r_{ij}\, l_{ij}[t]}_{\text{inflow net of loss}} \;-\; \sum_{m:\,j\to m} P_{jm}[t] \;+\; p_{ag_j}[t] \;+\; \mathbb{1}[j = 0]\; p_{import}[t] \;=\; 0 \tag{3.31} \]

plus the mirrored reactive balance \(R_{q,j}[t] = 0\) (3.32), the network constraints (3.33/3.36/3.39/3.43/3.45), and each aggregator's device constraints \(x_j \in \mathcal{X}_j\) (eqs. 3.2–3.9 from the devices section). Everything is affine except the concave quadratic objective and the second-order cones — a convex problem (“GLB-CVX”) with strong duality, which is the license for everything that follows.

Interpretation of the objective: total prosumer utility minus the DSO's net wholesale bill. That is a social-welfare function for the whole distribution area — the DSO is modeled as a benevolent coordinator here (the conceptual leader/follower story lives in the planning layer, not in this convex operational core).

The derivation: why the balance multiplier is a price

Introduce a multiplier \(\lambda_j[t]\) for each active balance (3.31) and \(\mu_j[t]\) for each reactive balance, and form the partial Lagrangian — dualizing only the balances while keeping the device sets \(\mathcal{X}_j\) and the network constraint set \(\mathcal{N}\) implicit:

\[ \mathcal{L} = \sum_j U_{ag_j}(x_j) - \sum_t \lambda_0[t]\, p_{import}[t] + \sum_{j,t} \lambda_j[t]\, R_{p,j}[t] + \sum_{j,t} \mu_j[t]\, R_{q,j}[t]. \]

The problem is convex and strictly feasible (Slater holds on these fixtures), so an optimal primal–dual pair \((x^\star, \lambda^\star, \mu^\star)\) forms a saddle point: \(x^\star\) maximizes \(\mathcal{L}(\cdot, \lambda^\star, \mu^\star)\) over the remaining constraints. Now read the stationarity conditions one variable at a time.

Step 1 — the frontier pins the root price to the MEM

\(p_{import}[t]\) appears exactly twice in \(\mathcal{L}\): in the objective with coefficient \(-\lambda_0[t]\), and in the root balance \(R_{p,0}[t]\) with coefficient \(+1\). For a free-sign frontier (the allow_export = true case) stationarity gives

\[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial p_{import}[t]} = -\lambda_0[t] + \lambda_0^{\,bus}[t] = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda_{root}[t] = \lambda_0[t]. \]

The dual at the root equals the wholesale price — derived, not imposed. (This is why the figure below shows the root's curve sitting exactly on the flat MEM price, and why the code's welfare accounting can legitimately use \(\text{dual}(\text{balance\_p}[root,t])\) as \(\lambda_0\).) With import-only (\(p_{import} \ge 0\)), the same condition holds whenever imports are strictly positive; the equality relaxes to \(\lambda_{root} \le \lambda_0\) only when the frontier constraint itself binds at zero.

Step 2 — the prosumer block separates, and \(\lambda_j\) decentralizes it

Collect every term of \(\mathcal{L}\) that involves aggregator \(j\)'s decisions \(x_j\). Its net injection \(p_{ag_j}[t]\) appears in exactly one balance — its own bus's (3.31), with coefficient \(+1\) — so those terms are

\[ \mathcal{L}_j(x_j) \;=\; U_{ag_j}(x_j) \;+\; \sum_t \lambda_j[t]\; p_{ag_j}[t](x_j) \;+\; \sum_t \mu_j[t]\; q_{ag_j}[t](x_j). \]

At the saddle point, \(x_j^\star\) must maximize \(\mathcal{L}_j\) over \(x_j \in \mathcal{X}_j\) — independently of every other bus and of the network variables, because given the multipliers, \(\mathcal{L}\) is additively separable across those blocks. But \(\max_{x_j \in \mathcal{X}_j} \mathcal{L}_j(x_j)\) is precisely the prosumer's own problem facing the nodal price \(\lambda_j\) (compare the prosumer problem stated at the top of the devices section: earn \(\lambda_j\) per unit injected, pay it per unit consumed). Writing the first-order condition for an interior consumption decision \(d_j[t] = -p_{ag_j}[t]\):

\[ \frac{\partial U_{ag_j}}{\partial d_j[t]} \;=\; \lambda_j[t] \]

— marginal utility of consumption equals the nodal price, the classic decentralization condition, holding here per bus and per hour. This is the whole theorem: announce \(\lambda_j^\star[t]\), let each prosumer selfishly optimize, and (by convexity and strong duality — no duality gap, no non-convex lower level, no MPEC) each one picks exactly its welfare-optimal schedule \(x_j^\star\). The price coordinates without commanding. The thesis's ADMM subproblem AGR-OPT (its eq. 3.46) is literally this block plus a proximal penalty \(-\tfrac{\rho}{2}\|R_{p,j}\|^2\); the ADMM dual update \(\lambda_j \leftarrow \lambda_j + \rho R_{p,j}\) is dual ascent toward exactly the \(\lambda^\star\) derived here — which is why the distributed solve and the centralized solve agree, and why the code can extract the DADP from either.

In code: solve_welfare registers the closed balance as ctx.constraints[:balance_p], and extract_dlmp(ctx) returns \(\lambda_j[t] = \text{dual}(\text{balance\_p}[j,t])\) — the full \((N_{bus} \times T)\) price matrix, read straight from the solver's dual solution. Positive \(\lambda_j[t]\) is the marginal social cost of consuming one more unit at that bus and hour.

DLMP anatomy: energy + loss + congestion + voltage

Why does \(\lambda_j\) differ from \(\lambda_0\) at all? Because between the root and bus \(j\) sit wires with resistance, thermal limits, and voltage bounds — and each contributes marginal pressure. To see it, apply stationarity once more, now to a branch flow \(P_b\) on branch \(b = (i \to j)\). \(P_b\) appears in: the child balance (\(+P_b\), dual \(\lambda_j\)); the parent balance (\(-P_b\), dual \(\lambda_i\)); the true voltage drop (3.33, coefficient \(2r_b\), dual \(\beta_b\)); the exactness-copy drop (3.43, coefficient \(2r_b\), dual \(\gamma_b\)); the rotated loss cone (3.39, P-slot of its conic dual, call it \(\sigma_b\)); and — where a genuine thermal limit exists — the apparent-power cone (3.36, P-slot dual \(\nu_b\)). Setting \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial P_b = 0\) and collecting terms yields the per-branch price increment the code certifies to machine precision on every solve:

\[ \lambda_j[t] - \lambda_i[t] \;=\; -\Bigl(\, \sigma_b[t] \;+\; \nu_b[t] \;+\; 2 r_b\bigl(\beta_b[t] + \gamma_b[t]\bigr) \Bigr) \]

where, in the code's terms, \(\sigma_b = \text{dual}(\text{cone}[b,t])[3]\) (the P-slot of the rotated SOC dual), \(\nu_b = \text{dual}(\text{smax}[b,t])[2]\), and \(\beta_b, \gamma_b\) are the duals of the registered :vdrop and :cpydrop equalities. Because the feeder is a radial tree, bus \(j\) has a unique path from the root, and summing the increment along that path telescopes — \(\sum_{b \in \text{path}} (\lambda_{child} - \lambda_{parent}) = \lambda_j - \lambda_0\) — attributing the whole nodal price to four independently sourced components:

\[ \lambda_j[t] \;=\; \underbrace{\lambda_0[t]}_{\text{energy}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{b\in\text{path}} -\,\sigma_b[t]}_{\text{loss (3.39)}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{b\in\text{path}} -\,\nu_b[t]}_{\text{congestion (3.36)}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{b\in\text{path}} -\,2r_b\bigl(\beta_b[t]+\gamma_b[t]\bigr)}_{\text{voltage (3.33/3.43)}} \]
  • Energy — the root's own dual, \(\text{dual}(\text{balance\_p}[root,t])\), identical at every node and equal to the MEM price \(\lambda_0\) by Step 1. Note the code sources it from the dual, not from the input \(\lambda_0\) label — keeping the decomposition a pure statement about the solved model.
  • Loss — the marginal-loss term, sourced from the rotated cone's dual: one more unit consumed at \(j\) changes the \(r\,l\) losses on every upstream branch, and this prices that change.
  • Congestion — the thermal-limit dual, identically zero on every branch whose apparent-power limit does not bind. In the code this term is structurally sparse: only branches with a genuine \(S_{max}\) (in the IEEE-13 fixture, the head branch) even get the cone, so interior branches cannot fabricate congestion rent.
  • Voltage — the propagated pressure of the voltage bounds, and an honest departure from the textbook: it contains two duals, \(\beta\) from the true drop and \(\gamma\) from the LinDistFlow exactness-copy drop (3.43). A derivation that ignores the exactness copy — which the naive branch-flow SOCP does not have — drops \(\gamma\) and no longer sums to the nodal price. Zero when no voltage headroom is engaged.

decompose_dlmp computes each component from its own distinct registered dual (loss is not the leftover after subtracting the others — a dropped term cannot hide) and then hard-asserts \(\text{energy}+\text{loss}+\text{congestion}+\text{voltage} \approx \text{dual}(\text{balance\_p})\) at every (bus, hour), throwing with the worst residual's location on failure. Reaching the returned NamedTuple is the validation.

The honest finding: losses can be worth negative money

Textbook intuition says the leaf of a feeder is the most expensive place to consume — energy must travel there, losing \(r\,l\) along the way. That is true under forward flow. But on the export-heavy fixture the docs page solves (PV-battery aggregators with allow_export = true, feeder running in reverse), a marginal unit consumed downstream relieves the reverse flow and therefore reduces branch losses: the marginal-loss component is genuinely negative, and the leaf bus is the cheapest node — the classic DLMP sign flip under reverse flow. This is not a bug to be smoothed over; it is the price signal doing its job, telling load to move to where it soaks up surplus PV (the thesis's own over-voltage story: DADP drops below the MEM price to absorb over-generation, rises above it under congestion).

The reactive price — a fifth signal, never summed

The reactive balance (3.32) has its own multiplier \(\mu_j[t]\), extracted by extract_reactive_dlmp as the dual of :balance_q. It is a separate unit of account — a price per unit of reactive power — and the code deliberately never folds it into the active decomposition's sum-back identity (decompose_dlmp reports it as an un-summed fifth field). One derivable curiosity: the root's reactive price is degenerate (\(\mu_{root} \approx 0\)), because the reactive frontier \(q_{import}\) is a free-sign variable with zero objective cost — its stationarity condition forces its balance's dual to zero. No reactive energy market exists at the substation in this model, and the math says so.

Practical notes: getting duals you can publish

  • Prices need an interior-point conic solver. The framework's product is the dual vector, so solver choice is a correctness decision, not a performance one. The factory routes SOCP solves to Clarabel with duality-gap tolerances pinned to \(10^{-8}\) (tol_gap_abs/tol_gap_rel in src/solver/factory.jl) — an IPM converges primal and dual together to high accuracy. First-order solvers like SCS reach coarse tolerances with noisy duals: fine for feasibility/scale scouting, banned for final DADPs or exactness certification. No model file names a solver; swapping backends is one factory line.
  • No exactness certificate, no price. If the SOC relaxation (3.39) is strict — the cone slack, \(l\) a fictitious over-current — every dual is physically meaningless. solve_welfare runs the exactness gate (assert_socp_exact!, checking \(l\,v \approx P^2+Q^2\) with a relative, base-free tolerance) after the solve and before any dual is read, stashing the certificate ctx.meta[:socp_maxgap]; extract_dlmp refuses to return prices (throws) if handed an :l-bearing context without that certificate. Relatedly, the free-sign export frontier is the exactness enabler: priced export makes the objective strictly decreasing in \(l\) (every unit of loss burns export revenue), which is what holds the cone tight in exactly the reverse-flow regimes the research targets.
  • Sign conventions under Max. JuMP's dual() follows the conic-duality convention, which does not flip with the objective sense (that is shadow_price's job). Rather than trusting a remembered convention, the framework pins the economic sign — positive \(\lambda_j\) = marginal cost of consumption — with a hand-solved 2-bus regression test, and the decomposition's minus signs above are certified by the sum-back assertion. When in doubt, derive on a toy and pin with a test.
  • The settlement books balance. welfare_accounting splits the solved welfare into a prosumer surplus \(\sum_j U_{ag_j} + \sum_{j,t}\lambda_j[t]\, p_{ag_j}[t]\) (an exporter earns the transfer, an importer pays it — thesis eq. 3.46 in the code's injection convention) and a DSO surplus \(-\sum_{j,t}\lambda_j[t]\, p_{ag_j}[t] - \sum_t \lambda_0[t]\, p_{import}[t]\) (eq. 3.47): the DSO collects the DLMP-minus-wholesale spread. The \(\lambda_j \cdot p_{ag_j}\) transfer cancels between the two, so \(\text{social} = \text{prosumer} + \text{dso} = \) the objective value — asserted, with the code documenting honestly that this identity catches dropped/one-sided terms but is algebraically blind to a consistently flipped transfer sign (the individual surplus signs are pinned by tests instead).

Reading the price curves

Guided reading, matching the docs page that generates it from a live solve:

Each downstream bus is displaced from it by the telescoped per-branch increments — the locational content of the price. On this export-heavy fixture the displacement is downward, and the deepest (leaf) bus is the cheapest: the reverse-flow sign flip discussed above. An import-dominated fixture would lift the leaf above \(\lambda_0\) instead.
  • Right panel. The leaf's increment \(\lambda_{leaf}[t] - \lambda_0[t]\) stacked by component. On this small, unconstrained fixture the congestion and voltage duals are numerically zero (no \(S_{max}\) or voltage bound binds), so the stack is honestly all negative marginal loss — the same numbers whose four-way sum-back decompose_dlmp hard-asserted before the figure could even be drawn.

Decentralization: ADMM / Dual Ascent

5.1 Why decompose at all?

The centralized welfare problem of the previous section (solve_welfare, the GLB-CVX social-welfare SOCP) has one awkward assumption baked into its very statement: somebody — in practice, the DSO — gets to see every prosumer's private device parameters. Battery capacities, thermostat comfort bands, PV panel sizes, willingness-to-pay coefficients: all of it sits inside one monolithic model. That is fine as a mathematical benchmark, but it is exactly what a transactive-energy market is designed to avoid. The theory's promise is that a price signal can coordinate the same optimum without anyone surrendering their private information.

The decomposition makes that promise concrete by splitting the monolith along the ownership boundary (thesis eqs. 3.46/3.47):

  • AGR-OPTj — one small QP per load bus \(j\), owned by that bus's aggregator. It contains the private device models (PV-battery, thermostatic load, 4-quadrant BESS) and the aggregator utility \(U_{\mathrm{ag},j}\). It never sees the network.
  • DSO-OPT — one whole-network SOCP, owned by the network operator. It contains the convex branch-flow constraints (KCL, voltage drop, the rotated cone, the exactness copy) and the priced frontier exchange \(p_{\mathrm{import}}[t]\) with the wholesale market at the MEM price \(\lambda_0[t]\). It never sees a device parameter.

The two problems talk to each other through exactly one physical fact: at every load bus and hour, the power the aggregator injects must equal the power the network carries away. In the code this is the nodal active balance (thesis eq. 3.31), written as a residual \(R_{p,j}[t] = \text{netflow}_j[t] + p_{\mathrm{ag},j}[t]\) that the centralized model pins to zero — and whose dual is the day-ahead dynamic price \(\lambda_j[t]\) (the DADP). ADMM turns that constraint into an iterative negotiation: each side optimizes privately against a trial price, and the price moves until the two sides agree.

5.2 The derivation, step by step

Step 1 — the centralized problem with the coupling made explicit

Write the centralized welfare problem, isolating the one constraint that ties the two ownership domains together:

\[ \max_{\substack{\text{device vars},\\ \text{network vars}}} \;\; \sum_j U_{\mathrm{ag},j} \;-\; \sum_t \lambda_0[t]\, p_{\mathrm{import}}[t] \quad\text{s.t.}\quad \underbrace{R_{p,j}[t] = \text{netflow}_j[t] + p_{\mathrm{ag},j}[t] = 0}_{\text{nodal balance (3.31)}}, \;\; \text{plus private and network constraints} \tag{5.1} \]

where \(p_{\mathrm{ag},j}[t] = \sum_d p^{\mathrm{inject}}_d[t] - P^{\mathrm{dc}}_j[t]\) is the aggregator's net injection (devices minus inelastic demand, thesis 3.22), and \(\text{netflow}_j[t]\) is the network-side expression at bus \(j\) (incident branch flows and losses). All device constraints involve only aggregator variables; all power-flow constraints involve only network variables. Only (5.1)'s balance mixes the two.

Step 2 — the augmented Lagrangian

Relax only the coupling constraint, keeping each side's own constraints inside its block. For a maximization problem the augmented Lagrangian adds a linear multiplier term and a quadratic penalty on the violation:

\[ L_\rho \;=\; \sum_j U_{\mathrm{ag},j} \;-\; \sum_t \lambda_0[t]\, p_{\mathrm{import}}[t] \;-\; \sum_j \sum_t \lambda_j[t]\, R_{p,j}[t] \;-\; \frac{\rho}{2} \sum_j \sum_t R_{p,j}[t]^2 \tag{5.2} \]

The multiplier \(\lambda_j[t]\) is the trial price at bus \(j\), hour \(t\); the penalty weight \(\rho > 0\) makes the Lagrangian strongly concave in the coupling direction, which is what lets alternating optimization converge where plain dual decomposition can oscillate.
