A sign warning, stated up front because the code is explicit about it: the internal multiplier of the \(-\lambda_j^\top R_{p,j}\) term converges to the negated centralized dual \(-\,\mathrm{dual}(\texttt{balance\_p}[j,t])\) under JuMP's equality-dual convention for a Max objective. The DADP the framework reports is the negation of the internal multiplier — verified empirically on the 2-bus fixture, where the analytic load-bus price is \(+\lambda_0\) and the raw internal multiplier lands at \(-\lambda_0\). Everything below is written in terms of the internal multiplier (what the loop actually updates); the published price flips its sign once, at the very end.

Step 3 — block 1: the aggregator subproblem AGR-OPTj

Freeze the network side at its last solved value: \(\text{netflow}_j = c_j\) (a plain constant vector). Then \(R_{p,j} = c_j + p_{\mathrm{ag},j}\), and the terms of (5.2) involving aggregator \(j\) alone become

\[ \text{AGR-OPT}_j:\quad \max_{\text{device vars}}\;\; U_{\mathrm{ag},j} \;-\; \sum_t \lambda_j[t]\, p_{\mathrm{ag},j}[t] \;-\; \frac{\rho}{2} \sum_t \bigl(c_j[t] + p_{\mathrm{ag},j}[t]\bigr)^2 \quad\text{s.t. device constraints} \tag{5.3} \]

This is thesis eq. 3.46. Two structural facts make it cheap to re-solve. First, it is separable per node — every aggregator solves independently (and privately). Second, expanding the penalty, \(-\tfrac{\rho}{2}(c + p)^2 = -\tfrac{\rho}{2}p^2 - \rho c\, p - \tfrac{\rho}{2}c^2\), shows the quadratic part \(-\tfrac{\rho}{2}p_{\mathrm{ag},j}[t]^2\) never changes between iterations; only the linear coefficient on \(p_{\mathrm{ag},j}[t]\) does:

\[ \text{coeff}\bigl(p_{\mathrm{ag},j}[t]\bigr) \;=\; -\lambda_j[t] \;-\; \rho\, c_j[t] \tag{5.4} \]

So each ADMM iteration touches one scalar objective coefficient per hour and re-solves — the model itself is built exactly once.

Step 4 — block 2: the network subproblem DSO-OPT

Now freeze the aggregator side at its just-solved value \(p_{\mathrm{ag},j} = a_j\), and give the network side its own explicit coupling variable by renaming \(p^{\mathrm{dso}}_j := -\text{netflow}_j\) (the network injection carries the opposite sign of the coupling variable — this renaming is the single most bug-prone sign in the whole file, and the source header derives it carefully). Then \(R_{p,j} = a_j - p^{\mathrm{dso}}_j\), and the remaining terms of (5.2), written as a minimization, become

\[ \text{DSO-OPT}:\quad \min_{\text{network vars}}\;\; \sum_t \lambda_0[t]\, p_{\mathrm{import}}[t] \;-\; \sum_j \sum_t \lambda_j[t]\, p^{\mathrm{dso}}_j[t] \;+\; \frac{\rho}{2} \sum_j \sum_t \bigl(p^{\mathrm{dso}}_j[t] - a_j[t]\bigr)^2 \quad\text{s.t. SOCP network constraints} \tag{5.5} \]

This is thesis eq. 3.47. By the same expansion as before, the per-iteration update is again a single linear coefficient per \((j,t)\): \(\text{coeff}(p^{\mathrm{dso}}_j[t]) = -\lambda_j[t] - \rho\, a_j[t]\). The frontier term \(\lambda_0^\top p_{\mathrm{import}}\) keeps the objective strictly decreasing in the branch loss variable \(\ell\), which is what keeps the SOC relaxation exact even under reverse flow (the PF-04 free-sign-export enabler from the SOCP section).

Step 5 — the dual update: tâtonnement, literally

With both blocks solved, take one gradient-ascent step on the multiplier along the coupling violation:

\[ \lambda_j[t] \;\leftarrow\; \lambda_j[t] \;+\; \rho\, R_{p,j}[t], \qquad R_{p,j}[t] = a_j[t] - p^{\mathrm{dso}}_j[t] \tag{5.6} \]

and refresh the AGR target for the next round, \(c_j[t] = -\,p^{\mathrm{dso}}_j[t]\) (the sign renaming of Step 4 again). The step size equals the penalty \(\rho\) — the standard ADMM choice that makes the second block's iterate dual-feasible by construction.

Economic reading. Undo the internal sign (published DADP \(=-\lambda_j\)) and (5.6) says: at a bus-hour where the aggregator wants to withdraw more power than the network's optimal dispatch delivers there (consensus violated on the demand side), the published price rises; where the aggregator injects more than the network can profitably carry away, the price falls. That is Walrasian tâtonnement performed by an algorithm: no auctioneer, just a multiplier climbing its constraint's violation. At the fixed point \(R_{p,j} = 0\), the DSO's own internal balance dual equals \(\lambda_j\), so the converged coupling price coincides with the centralized DADP \(\mathrm{dual}(\texttt{balance\_p}[j,t])\) — the same price, discovered without ever pooling the private data.

Step 6 — residuals and the stopping rule

Two quantities certify convergence (Boyd et al., §3.3; thesis App. B.30–B.32 in unscaled form), both 2-norms over all \(p = n_{\mathrm{load}} \cdot T\) coupling entries:

\[ \|r^k\|_2 = \Bigl(\textstyle\sum_{j,t} \bigl(a_j[t] - p^{\mathrm{dso}}_j[t]\bigr)^2\Bigr)^{1/2}, \qquad \|s^k\|_2 = \rho \,\bigl\| p^{\mathrm{dso},\,k} - p^{\mathrm{dso},\,k-1} \bigr\|_2 \tag{5.7} \]

The primal residual \(r\) is the raw consensus mismatch — how far apart the two blocks still are. The dual residual \(s\) is the change in the second-updated block (the \(z\)-block in Boyd's notation, here DSO-OPT's coupling variable) scaled by \(\rho\) — it measures whether the price has stopped moving. The stopping thresholds are per-unit normalized from the two tolerances \(\varepsilon_{abs}\) and \(\varepsilon_{rel}\):

\[ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{pri}} = \sqrt{p}\,\varepsilon_{abs} + \varepsilon_{rel}\max\bigl(\|a\|_2, \|p^{\mathrm{dso}}\|_2\bigr), \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{dual}} = \sqrt{p}\,\varepsilon_{abs} + \varepsilon_{rel}\,\|\lambda\|_2 \tag{5.8} \]

and the loop stops only when both \(\|r\| \le \varepsilon_{\mathrm{pri}}\) and \(\|s\| \le \varepsilon_{\mathrm{dual}}\). This is deliberate: stopping on the primal residual alone is the textbook false-convergence bug — the two blocks can momentarily agree while the price is still in flight. (The framework's own Phase-6 prototype made exactly this mistake, tracking \(\rho\,\Delta a\), the change in the first block — the wrong block — and Phase 7 corrected it; the residual ledger's docstrings document the correction.) If maxiter is reached without both residuals below threshold, solve_admm throws loudly, naming all four numbers — it never silently returns a non-consensus iterate as if it were a price.

Step 7 — the reactive mirror (Phase 19, reactive_consensus = :live)

By default the reactive channel is not negotiated at all: each load node's reactive draw is the inelastic constant \(-P^{\mathrm{dc}}_j[t]\tan(\arccos\varphi_j)\) (thesis 3.23, assumption A3). But when a device with a genuine reactive decision (a 4-quadrant BESS) is present, the loop runs a second, jointly-converging dual-ascent block built by the identical AGR-fixes-target / DSO-renames-coupling-variable construction, merely on the reactive axis:

\[ \mu^{\mathrm{int}}_j[t] \;\leftarrow\; \mu^{\mathrm{int}}_j[t] \;+\; \rho_q\, R_{q,j}[t], \qquad R_{q,j}[t] = b_j[t] - q^{\mathrm{dso}}_j[t] \tag{5.9} \]

with its own penalty \(\rho_q\) (adapted independently — the reactive channel is typically much smaller-scaled than the active one, so a shared \(\rho\) would be badly conditioned for it). The published reactive price is again the negated internal multiplier, \(\mu_j[t] = -\mu^{\mathrm{int}}_j[t]\), converging to the centralized \(\mathrm{dual}(\texttt{balance\_q}[j,t])\) — the same sign relationship \(\lambda\) has to :balance_p, verified empirically on a 2-bus + 4Q-BESS fixture with non-negligible impedance. Crucially, the stopping rule under live-reactive mode is one stacked norm over both coupling axes — a single \(r/s/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pri}}/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{dual}}\) test over the concatenated \((\lambda, \mu)\) blocks, never two independent per-block checks (Boyd's multi-block caveat: independent checks can declare one block converged while the other's motion keeps perturbing it).

5.3 Engineering that makes it converge in practice

These are the load-bearing implementation decisions, all of them visible in the source:

  • Build once, re-solve many. Both AGR-OPT and DSO-OPT are constructed once, outside the loop. No Model(...) call appears in the loop body; num_variables/num_constraints are iteration-count-independent. Each iteration mutates only the linear objective coefficients (5.4) via set_objective_coefficient — one scalar per bus-hour.
  • The price is deliberately not a JuMP Parameter. A \(\lambda \cdot p_{\mathrm{ag}}\) Parameter-times-variable term is an indefinite bilinear that the convex conic backend rejects. The prices live as plain Float64s folded into objective coefficients. (JuMP Parameters are the right tool elsewhere in the framework — for constraint RHS data like initial conditions and forecasts in the MPC window model of the next section — just not for a price multiplying a variable in the objective.)
  • Warm starts, honestly. Clarabel is a copy-to-only backend, so solver-level warm starts are a no-op here — the build-once win is eliminating the JuMP-side rebuild, not solver warm starting. The warm start that does matter is the multiplier initialization: the internal \(\lambda\) starts at \(-\lambda_0\) (the DADP is \(\lambda_0\) plus small loss/congestion/voltage terms, so \(-\lambda_0\) puts the internal multiplier right next to its fixed point). Initializing at \(+\lambda_0\) — the tempting sign — puts it a distance \(\approx 2\lambda_0\) away and was measured to cost 100+ iterations on the congested IEEE-13 versus ~10 with the correct sign.
  • Adaptive \(\rho\) by residual balancing (Boyd §3.4.1, with one deliberate twist). The \(\rho\) keyword is only the initial penalty \(\rho_0\). Each iteration compares the two residuals and re-balances: \(\rho \leftarrow \tau\rho\) if the primal lags, \(\rho \leftarrow \rho/\tau\) if the dual lags (defaults \(\tau_{\mathrm{ratio}} = 2\), imbalance band \(\mu = 10\)), clamped to \([\rho_{\min}, \rho_{\max}]\). The twist: the comparison uses \(\varepsilon\)-normalized residuals \(\hat r = \|r\|/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pri}}\), \(\hat s = \|s\|/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{dual}}\), not the raw norms Boyd's recipe compares. On these problems \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pri}}\) (proportional to tiny per-unit injections) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{dual}}\) (proportional to \(\|\lambda\|\), an O(1–10) price) differ by ~50×, so the raw comparison reads "balanced" while the primal is 60× over its own tolerance — leaving \(\rho\) too small to regularize the DSO SOCP (measured: Clarabel NUMERICAL_ERROR by iteration 3 on IEEE-13). Normalizing each residual by its own threshold makes the balancing dimensionless, and the same \((\varepsilon_{abs}, \varepsilon_{rel}, \tau, \mu)\) then converge the 2-bus, IEEE-13 and IEEE-123 cases with no scale-specific tuning. Once both normalized residuals are within 10× of tolerance, \(\rho\) freezes — Boyd's convergence theory assumes \(\rho\) eventually constant, and freezing prevents late-stage oscillation from stalling the tail. On an actual \(\rho\) change, set_rho! mutates the quadratic penalty coefficients in place (build-once preserved); \(\lambda\) itself is never rescaled — it is the unscaled physical price, not the scaled multiplier \(u = \lambda/\rho\) of scaled-form ADMM.
  • Why \(\rho_0 = 100\) on the default scenario. The Scenario default is the empirically-validated initial penalty for the congested IEEE-13 + default-population case: starting the adaptive loop at \(\rho_0 = 1\) numerically errors on that fixture before residual balancing can climb \(\rho\) to a well-conditioned value. Adaptive \(\rho\) still self-tunes from whatever starting point it is given; \(\rho_0\) just has to be survivable.
  • Certificates run at the converged point, not mid-loop. Mid-loop iterates are legitimately off-consensus (the battery co-activates at a not-yet-correct price; the SOC cone is legitimately loose), so the exactness and complementarity gates would spuriously fail there. At convergence a final consolidation pass re-solves both blocks with all gates on: the PF-04 SOC-exactness gate on DSO-OPT (exact_maxgap), the App. C battery complementarity check per aggregator, and a physical no-slack certificate on every :balance_p row (recomputed from the primal, independent of the solver's OPTIMAL/ALMOST label). Welfare is recomputed from primals, \(\sum_j U_{\mathrm{ag},j} - \lambda_0^\top p_{\mathrm{import}}\) — never the \(\rho\)-penalized subproblem objective.
  • The cross-validation that makes the whole thing trustworthy (ADMM-04). The same scenario is solved centrally and by ADMM, and the two must agree: on the documentation build's 3-bus fixture the welfare gap is computed live at order \(10^{-8}\) and the converged \(\lambda_j[t]\) match the centralized DADP duals at order \(10^{-7}\); the hard isapprox regression gates live in the test suite. Since the decomposed loop and the centralized solve share no solution path, agreement at that precision is a genuine correctness certificate for both.

Known limitations (stated plainly)

  • The loop assumes a 1:1 node↔aggregator coupling — one aggregator per load bus. Several aggregators sharing a bus would make the netflow target \(c_j\) ambiguous to split; the guard throws.
  • It requires allow_export = true (the free-sign priced frontier is the SOC-exactness enabler); an import-only frontier is refused.
  • A 4Q-BESS's individual \(q\)-trajectory is not cross-validated against the centralized solve: when the reactive dual \(\mu \approx 0\) (a lightly-loaded reactive channel), the device's own P–Q split inside its apparent-power cone is non-unique — welfare, \(\lambda\), and \(\mu\) are compared; a degenerate quantity is not pinned.

5.4 Reading the convergence figure

The figure plots \(\|r^k\|_2\) and \(\|s^k\|_2\) per iteration on a logarithmic axis, with the per-unit thresholds \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{pri}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{dual}}\) drawn as reference lines. How to read it:

  1. The first iterations are large by construction. The dual-residual snapshot initializes at zero, so iteration 1's \(s = \rho\|p^{\mathrm{dso},1}\|\) is deliberately big — a one-iteration budget can never false-converge.
  2. Look for the roughly linear descent on the log axis — dual ascent with a well-conditioned \(\rho\) converges linearly; kinks in the slope line up with adaptive-\(\rho\) changes (the \(\rho\) trace is recorded alongside, and each doubling/halving visibly re-balances which residual leads).
  3. The two curves need not cross their thresholds together. Often the primal residual dives first (the blocks agree) while the dual residual — the price still settling — lags a few iterations. The stop fires only when both are below their lines; the gap between those two events is exactly the false-convergence window a primal-only stop would fall into.
  4. The threshold lines themselves move slightly: (5.8) makes them relative to the current iterate norms, so they drift as \(\|a\|, \|\lambda\|\) settle.

Where it lives

  • src/admm/solve_admm.jl — the hand-rolled outer loop: dual ascent (5.6)/(5.9), residuals (5.7), thresholds (5.8), adaptive \(\rho\), the fail-loud cap, the final consolidation gates, and the sign-convention derivations in the file header.
  • src/admm/AgrOpt.jl — build_agr_opt/solve_agr!: the per-node QP (5.3), built once, re-solved by one objective-coefficient write per hour.
  • src/admm/DsoOpt.jl — build_dso_opt/solve_dso!: the whole-network SOCP (5.5) reusing ConvexBranchFlow.contribute! verbatim, with the explicit coupling variable \(p^{\mathrm{dso}}_j\) and the registered :balance_p/:balance_q duals.
  • src/admm/residuals.jl — AdmmResiduals: the JuMP-free per-iteration ledger (\(r, s, \rho, \varepsilon_{\mathrm{pri}}, \varepsilon_{\mathrm{dual}}\), price gap) and the two-residual converged predicate.
  • src/admm/ReactiveMode.jl — the OFF / CERTIFIED / LIVE three-state reactive mode and its normalization.

See it run

Docs page "Rung 5: ADMM Decomposition" (built from docs/literate/admm.jl): it solves the same 3-bus, two-aggregator scenario centrally and by ADMM during the documentation build, displays the live welfare gap and the PF-04 exactness certificate, and renders the convergence figure above — every number recomputed, never hardcoded.

Operational Extensions

Everything so far solves one day-ahead problem and reports one set of prices, on a radial feeder, under perfect foresight. The three extensions in this section relax those assumptions one at a time — and each is deliberately built as an independent sibling of the day-ahead pipeline, not a rewrite of it: the same validated device and network builders are reused verbatim, and only the orchestration around them changes.

6.1 MPC / rolling-horizon real-time pricing

Motivation

A day-ahead price is a forecast-conditional promise. Real operation deviates: PV comes in under or over forecast, demand drifts. The receding-horizon (MPC) extension asks the practical question — what does the price signal look like when the operator re-optimizes as reality unfolds? — and, just as importantly, how much welfare does closing the loop cost relative to the perfect-foresight day-ahead optimum?

The formulation delta vs the day-ahead base

The day-ahead base solves one welfare problem over \(t = 1,\dots,T\). The MPC variant (run_mpc(s::Scenario)) instead builds one fixed-length window model over window-local hours \(\tau = 1,\dots,H\) (default \(H=6\)) — the same welfare-shaped objective and constraint set — and re-solves it at absolute hours \(t = 1, 1+\Delta, 1+2\Delta, \dots\) (step \(\Delta = \texttt{mpc\_step}\), default 1). Three things change per re-solve, and only these three; the model is never rebuilt:

  1. State initial conditions — battery SOC and thermostatic indoor temperature enter as JuMP Parameters (soc0/Tin0), set to the measured (propagated) state at hour \(t\).
  2. Forecast data slices — PV, ambient temperature, and inelastic demand over \([t, t+H-1]\) enter as Parameter vectors (Ppv_param/Tout_param/Pdc_param).
  3. The MEM price slice \(\lambda_0[t{:}t{+}H{-}1]\) — slid via set_objective_coefficient on \(p_{\mathrm{import}}[\tau]\), never a Parameter (a price-times-variable Parameter term is a bilinear the convex backend rejects — the same pitfall as in the ADMM section).

Forecast error is injected as a seeded, bounded multiplicative perturbation: at each resolve a deterministic sub-seeded draw produces factors \((f_{\mathrm{pv}}, f_{\mathrm{dem}})\) within \(\pm\,\texttt{mpc\_forecast\_error}\) (default \(\pm 5\%\)), applied to the PV and demand slices the optimizer sees. Ambient temperature slides unperturbed — model mismatch enters only through the declared forecast-error channel, never through the deterministic window slide.

The mechanism, step by step

  1. Two one-time day-ahead benchmarks are solved first, outside the loop, both at the full \(T\): (a) the full-population perfect-foresight reference, producing day_ahead_welfare and the reference DADP path \(\lambda^{\mathrm{DA}}_j[t]\); and (b) a comparable benchmark over exactly the device set the closed loop controls, which the regret comparison reads (see the honesty note below).
  2. Per resolve at hour \(t\): set the IC Parameters from measured state; set the terminal-SOC target Parameter (below); slide the perturbed forecast slices and the \(\lambda_0\) coefficients; optimize!.
  3. Certify and price the solved window through a non-throwing certificate ladder (below), producing a price vector for the window and a status symbol.
  4. Publish and apply the first \(n_{\mathrm{apply}} = \min(\Delta, H, \dots)\) hours: record the published real-time price \(\lambda^{\mathrm{RTP}}_j[t]\) (window position \(\tau=1,\dots\)) into the trace alongside the day-ahead reference at the same absolute hour, accumulate realized welfare from the applied controls, and propagate the measured state hour by hour — SOC through the charge/discharge recursion, indoor temperature through the thermal recursion anchored on the ground-truth ambient (state propagation is truth-anchored even though settlement is not; see caveats).
  5. Regret, at the end: realized welfare minus the day-ahead benchmark's welfare restricted to the same published \(k = T-H+1\) decision hours and the same device set. The published-hour count is always \(T - H + 1\) regardless of \(\Delta\) — a larger step only shrinks the number of resolves, never the published horizon.

Why the terminal-SOC condition exists (battery myopia)

A window model that ends at hour \(t + H - 1\) believes the world ends there. An unconstrained battery would therefore dump all stored energy before the artificial horizon (its value past the window is invisible), or symmetrically hoard when prices within the window are unattractive — and each subsequent resolve would inherit a distorted state. The fix implemented here is the textbook hard terminal-equality constraint (as opposed to a terminal cost/penalty term):

\[ \mathrm{soc}[H] \;=\; \mathrm{soc}^{\mathrm{DA}}\bigl[\min(t + H - 1,\; T)\bigr] \tag{6.1} \]

— the window's final SOC is pinned, via a re-settable Parameter, to the comparable day-ahead benchmark's own optimal SOC trajectory at the corresponding absolute hour. Pinning to the benchmark trajectory (rather than an arbitrary target) keeps the closed loop and the regret benchmark on the same information footing. The toggle is build-time: with mpc_terminal_soc = false the constraint genuinely does not exist in the model — a different model, not a silent no-op — and the framework's tests carry the A/B negative control showing the dump/hoard pathology it prevents (a measured ~35,530× separation margin on the test fixture). Guards: the pin requires \(H \ge 2\) (at \(H = 1\) it would double-pin \(\mathrm{soc}[1]\) against the IC), and with stateful devices the step must satisfy \(\Delta \le H - 1\), because the window's \(H\)-th control carries no modeled state consequence — applying it can drive the propagated state out of bounds and make the next resolve infeasible.

The certificate / fallback ladder

Every resolve's published price is a dual, and a dual is only trustworthy if the SOC relaxation is exact for that window. The per-resolve check is a non-throwing escalation ladder — the closed loop must never die mid-day:

  1. Tier 1 — inline cone check: the same per-branch cone-residual formula as the centralized exactness gate, at the same tolerances (rtol \(10^{-4}\), atol \(10^{-6}\)), but computed inline without throwing. Pass ⇒ status :certified_convex_dual, price \(= \mathrm{dual}(\texttt{balance\_p})\) of the window itself.
  2. Tier 2 — restricted rescue: a one-off solve of the same window under the RestrictedBranchFlow formulation plus an AC cross-solve and its own exactness certificate (in report mode). Pass ⇒ status :certified_convex_dual_restricted — a deliberately distinct provenance symbol, because the price now comes from the restricted solve's dual. Each escalation re-prices the same window: same absolute hours, same measured state, same forecast perturbation.
  3. Tier 3 — local AC dual: ac_dual_fallback_price, a nonconvex AC solve's local dual ⇒ status :local_ac_dual.
  4. Terminal — :cert_failed: if every tier fails, the published price for that resolve falls back to the day-ahead reference DADP slice, each tier's failure reason is warned (never swallowed), and the loop continues.

On the demonstration fixture every one of the 19 resolves certifies at Tier 1; the deeper tiers are exercised in the test suite on a deliberately forced-inexact high-PV fixture (cone ratio ≈9157× over threshold), not fabricated on the docs page.

Honest caveats

  • Settlement is forecast-consistent, not truth-settled. Realized welfare charges the window's own solved \(p_{\mathrm{import}}[\tau]\) — the import that balanced the perturbed forecast the optimizer saw — not a re-settled import against the ground truth. Under large forecast error a small positive regret is therefore possible as an artifact of this documented convention, not a free lunch. (Only state propagation is truth-anchored.) Truth-re-settlement is explicitly deferred.
  • The window structurally cannot host a Deferrable device (its energy-budget window is baked against the full day). The closed loop and the regret benchmark both run over a Deferrable-excluded population; the separately reported full-population day-ahead welfare is not directly comparable to realized welfare — only the restricted regret comparison is. An earlier revision that mixed the two populations systematically biased the regret in the MPC's favor; the fix (both sides read from the comparable benchmark) is documented in the source.
  • The escalation tiers lack the terminal-SOC pin (the generic welfare solver has no terminal hook) — an accepted, rare-path approximation.
  • The last \(H-1\) hours of the day are never published under the fixed-window convention — they fall inside the final window but after its first interval.

Reading the figure

Top panel: the dashed curve is the perfect-foresight day-ahead DADP over all 24 hours; the published real-time prices sit on top of it at their absolute hours. Where the two coincide, the rolling re-optimization confirmed the day-ahead signal; where they split, forecast error and the receding window genuinely moved the marginal price. The shaded region is the never-published tail. Bottom panel: the per-hour absolute gap \(|\lambda^{\mathrm{RTP}}[t] - \lambda^{\mathrm{DA}}[t]|\) as bars, with the running cumulative deviation as a line — the hour-by-hour version of the scalar price-consistency metrics (max_jump/mean_jump, the largest and mean absolute price move between successive published hours).

Where it lives / see it run

  • src/experiments/mpc_loop.jl — run_mpc, the certificate ladder (_mpc_certify_and_price), regret accounting, state propagation.
  • src/models/mpc_window.jl — build_mpc_window/MpcWindow: the build-once window model and its Parameter handles.
  • Docs page "Rung 8: MPC / Rolling-Horizon RTP" (docs/literate/mpc_rolling_horizon.jl).

6.2 Stochastic PV/demand uncertainty

Motivation

The MPC loop reacts to uncertainty after the fact. The stochastic extension plans for it: instead of optimizing against one PV/demand realization, commit a single battery schedule that is good in expectation across several possible tomorrows — and then honestly measure how that committed schedule performs on tomorrows it never saw.

The formulation delta: a two-stage extensive form

run_stochastic(s::Scenario) materializes \(S\) in-sample scenarios (\(3 \le S \le 5\)), each an independently seeded draw of the first-order Markov-chain profile generator (PV availability, demand, ambient — generate_profiles with disjoint sub-seed tags per scenario, so every scenario's draw is deterministic and distinct). All \(S\) scenarios are then assembled into one JuMP model — the extensive form — with the probability-weighted expected-welfare objective:

\[ \max \;\; \sum_{s=1}^{S} p_s \Bigl( \sum_j U^{(s)}_{\mathrm{ag},j} \;-\; \sum_t \lambda_0[t]\, p^{(s)}_{\mathrm{import}}[t] \Bigr), \qquad p_s > 0,\;\; \textstyle\sum_s p_s = 1 \tag{6.2} \]

where scenario \(s\) owns a complete, independent copy of the network constraints and device constraints, built against its own exogenous draw. (A mechanical aside the construction depends on: the branch-flow builder registers named JuMP containers, so building \(S\) copies on one model requires JuMP.unregister-ing the container names between scenario blocks — the variable handles themselves stay alive in each scenario's own context.)

Non-anticipativity: what is first-stage, what is recourse

In the code's actual formulation the first-stage/second-stage split is a device split, not a temporal split — a deliberate deviation from the textbook two-stage picture where "stage 1" is everything before an information reveal:

  • First-stage (here-and-now, shared across scenarios): the entire battery schedule — \(p_{\mathrm{ch}}[t]\), \(p_{\mathrm{dch}}[t]\) for every battery-like device (anything carrying an SOC state: PVBattery, FourQuadBESS), and for a 4Q-BESS also its reactive dispatch \(q[t]\). The battery commits its whole-day plan before knowing which scenario materializes.
  • Recourse (per-scenario): network flows and voltages, the frontier import \(p^{(s)}_{\mathrm{import}}\), and the thermostatic response — these adapt freely to each scenario's own draw.

Non-anticipativity is enforced by explicit equality constraints tying every scenario's battery copy to scenario 1's (the standard extensive-form idiom):

\[ p^{(s)}_{\mathrm{ch}}[t] = p^{(1)}_{\mathrm{ch}}[t], \quad p^{(s)}_{\mathrm{dch}}[t] = p^{(1)}_{\mathrm{dch}}[t], \quad \bigl(q^{(s)}[t] = q^{(1)}[t]\bigr) \qquad s = 2,\dots,S,\;\; t = 1,\dots,T \tag{6.3} \]

Two implementation details worth noticing. The SOC trajectory itself is deliberately not tied: each copy's initial condition plus its recursion, together with (6.3), already imply \(\mathrm{soc}^{(s)}[t] = \mathrm{soc}^{(1)}[t]\) — the explicit rows would be exactly linearly dependent, and \((S-1)\cdot T\) redundant equalities per battery are a needless interior-point conditioning hazard. And the builder enforces strict structural congruence across scenarios (same aggregator buses, same device counts and types at each index): without it, a mismatched scenario could silently leave a battery untied — a clairvoyant recourse battery that would quietly corrupt the two-stage solution.

Prices: per-scenario DADPs are primary; the expectation is derived

Each scenario's network copy has its own :balance_p constraints, so each scenario has its own DADP. One subtlety: in objective (6.2) scenario \(s\)'s constraints enter weighted by \(p_s\), so the raw dual is scaled by \(p_s\) relative to the deterministic case. The reported per-scenario price de-scales it:

\[ \lambda^{(s)}_j[t] \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{dual}\bigl(\texttt{balance\_p}^{(s)}[j,t]\bigr)}{p_s}, \qquad \bar\lambda_j[t] \;=\; \sum_{s} p_s\, \lambda^{(s)}_j[t] \tag{6.4} \]

The per-scenario vectors \(\lambda^{(s)}\) are the primary output — each scenario's agents face their own scenario's price. The probability-weighted expectation \(\bar\lambda\) is an explicitly labelled derived summary: it is not the dual of any constraint in the model, no agent ever faces it, and treating it as a tradeable price would discard exactly the scenario-conditionality the model exists to represent. SOCP exactness is likewise certified per scenario, never aggregated — one scenario's tight cone can never mask another's gap.

Out-of-sample evaluation

  1. Read the solved shared battery schedule off scenario 1's variables (by (6.3), scenario 1's copy is the committed schedule).
  2. Materialize \(H_{\mathrm{oos}}\) held-out scenarios (\(5 \le H_{\mathrm{oos}} \le 10\)) from a second, disjoint sub-seed tag family — no held-out draw ever replays an in-sample one.
  3. Build one evaluation harness (a single-scenario welfare model with the battery controls pinned by Parameter equalities), pin the controls to the committed schedule once (active pins clamped at 0 to absorb interior-point noise like \(p_{\mathrm{ch}} = -10^{-12}\)), then for each held-out draw slide only the PV/demand/ambient data Parameters and re-solve — build-once, re-solve \(H_{\mathrm{oos}}\) times.
  4. Report \(\;\texttt{welfare\_gap} = \frac{1}{|F|}\sum_{h \in F} W_h \;-\; W_{\mathrm{in\text{-}sample}}\;\) — the uniform-weight average realized welfare over the feasible held-out draws \(F\), minus the in-sample expected-welfare objective.

A held-out draw can be genuinely infeasible against the committed schedule — the classic committed-first-stage evaluation problem: if a held-out PV draw at some hour falls below every in-sample draw, the pinned \(p_{\mathrm{ch}}[t]\) collides with that draw's own PV availability bound. Such a draw is skipped-and-reported (NaN welfare, an infeasibility mask, a warning), never silently absorbed and never allowed to abort the run.

Honest caveats

  • The in-sample expected welfare and the out-of-sample realized average are differently weighted (probability-weighted vs uniform); welfare_gap is the defined comparison, not a naive subtraction of like-for-like numbers.
  • The gap's sign does not generalize: the docs fixture measures a small positive gap (the schedule slightly over-performs out of sample), the CI golden fixture a small negative one — both a fraction of a percent of the welfare scale. This is a mild demonstration, not a stress test of out-of-sample robustness.
  • The solve sits on a documented numerical knife-edge: probability weighting weakens a low-probability scenario's own loss-cost gradient, so the builder requests a tighter Clarabel gap tolerance (\(5 \times 10^{-10}\), swept to sit inside the window that converges cleanly on both a near-lossless and a lossy fixture), and even so, a particular uniform-spaced probability vector trips the convergence gate on the \(T=9\) docs fixture while other vectors solve cleanly. The project reports these findings rather than tuning them away.
  • \(\lambda_0\) is materialized once from scenario 1's profile draw and reused everywhere — legitimate only because the MEM price shape is deterministic and profile-independent; a profile-dependent price rule would need per-scenario prices.
  • Deferrable is not first-stage in this builder (deliberately excluded from the tie).

Reading the figures

The scenario fan shows the five exogenous draws the extensive form co-optimizes over — regenerated bit-identically from the same seeds the solve used. Note the non-uniform probability weights (a bell shape peaking at the central scenarios): the expectation in (6.2) and (6.4) leans toward those curves.

At full price scale the five DADP paths nearly coincide — this fixture's scenario-conditional price variation is real but modest, and the page says so. The deviation panel is where the structure lives: identically zero spread at hour 1 (every scenario's price floor binds the same way off-peak), genuine divergence around the mid-horizon hours — exactly the conditionality the derived expectation would erase.

Each dot is one held-out re-solve of the pinned schedule; an infeasible draw would simply be absent, never plotted as a fabricated point. The tiny distance between the two horizontal lines is the welfare gap — sub-percent on this fixture.

Where it lives / see it run

  • src/models/stochastic_welfare.jl — build_stochastic_welfare (the extensive form, non-anticipativity ties, per-scenario dual de-scaling) and StochasticOosHarness.
  • src/experiments/run_stochastic.jl — run_stochastic: seeded scenario materialization, schedule commitment, the held-out loop, the infeasibility mask.
  • src/data/profiles.jl — the seeded first-order Markov profile generator.
  • Docs page "Rung 9: Stochastic PV/Demand Uncertainty" (docs/literate/stochastic_pv_demand.jl).

6.3 Meshed networks and the live reactive price

Motivation: what breaks when the network has loops

Every exactness result the framework's price recovery rests on is a radial result: on a tree, the branch-flow SOCP relaxation is provably exact under the free-sign priced frontier, so its duals are trustworthy prices. On a meshed network the theory changes character in a subtle and dangerous way: the meshed SOCP is always conic-feasible (Low, arXiv:1405.0814) — the per-branch cone can be tight at the optimum and yet the solution can be physically meaningless, because branch-flow variables on a mesh drop the voltage angles, and a cone-tight flow pattern may admit no consistent angle assignment around a loop. The cone-tightness gate that certifies radial solutions is therefore uninformative on a mesh. Something else is needed.

What the meshed rung actually builds

The formulation itself required zero new constraint code: MeshedFeeder admits non-tree topologies, and MeshedFlow is a pure delegation to the existing ConvexBranchFlow constraint set (KCL, voltage drop, rotated cone, exactness copy, apparent-power cone). What is genuinely new is a fixture discovery and a certificate.

The odd-cycle degeneracy (a real, derived incompatibility). The formulation carries both the true squared voltage \(v\) and its exactness copy \(\hat v\), with both pinned to the same value at the root. Subtracting the two voltage-drop recursions and summing them around any closed cycle with branch orientations \(\epsilon_b = \pm 1\) forces

\[ \sum_{b \in \text{cycle}} \epsilon_b \,\bigl(r_b^2 + x_b^2\bigr)\, \ell_b \;=\; 0 \tag{6.5} \]

On an odd, consistently-oriented cycle (e.g. a literal 3-bus triangle) every \(\epsilon_b = +1\), and since every loss term \(\ell_b \ge 0\), identity (6.5) forces \(\ell_b = 0\) — hence \(P_b = Q_b = 0\) — on every loop branch: the model cannot carry any power around such a cycle, and even an infinitesimal asymmetric load is infeasible. The docs page reproduces this infeasibility live (and fails its own build if the claim ever regresses). The committed fixture is instead a 4-bus diamond (root branching to two buses that merge at a fourth): its cycle is even-length with a mixed \(\epsilon\) split \((+1,+1,-1,-1)\), turning (6.5) into a genuine, non-degenerate balance between the two parallel paths. A fixture-topology choice, not a formulation change.

The angle-recoverability certificate

Both impedance profiles of the diamond solve OPTIMAL and both pass the per-branch cone gate — demonstrating, concretely, that cone tightness cannot distinguish a genuine AC operating point from a loop-inconsistent one. The missing check is certify_angle_recoverable!: an a-posteriori test of the Farivar–Low angle-recovery condition, operationalized on the mesh's chords — around each independent loop, the angle differences implied by the solved branch flows must close consistently. Its verdicts on the two committed profiles:

  • Uniform impedances: certified (:angle_certified, worst chord residual ≈ 0.0063) — the full voltage-phasor field is returned; the solution is a genuine AC operating point.
  • Heterogeneous impedances (the same R/X ratios at 8× magnitude): unrecoverable (:angle_unrecoverable, worst residual ≈ 0.0607, a ≈9.7× separation) — no angle field exists; the solved objective remains a valid upper bound on the true AC welfare optimum, never a certified operating point (the relaxation's feasible set contains every genuine AC point, so its welfare maximum can only be ≥ the true AC maximum).

The certificate is deliberately report-by-default — an unrecoverable verdict is a scientific finding on this rung, not a defect to abort a run over (a warning, not an error). A topology-specific measured finding worth repeating honestly: on this diamond's parallel-two-path topology it is impedance magnitude, not R/X ratio spread, that separates the certificate's two branches — ratio heterogeneity alone did not.

The reactive price \(\mu_j[t]\), live on the mesh

Combining the meshed loop with the 4-quadrant BESS device makes the reactive price a first-class output. Read carefully what the code does and does not do here:

  • On the meshed rung, no meshed ADMM is built. The meshed SOCP is solved as a single centralized problem, and the reactive price is read directly off the solved model: \(\mu_j[t] = \mathrm{dual}(\texttt{balance\_q}[j,t])\) — the genuine convex dual of one monolithic solve.
  • The iterative counterpart exists on radial feeders (Phase 19): as derived in the ADMM section, solve_admm(...; reactive_consensus = :live) runs the second, jointly-converging \(\mu\)-ascent block whose internal multiplier converges to \(-\mathrm{dual}(\texttt{balance\_q}[j,t])\), the same quantity up to the reporting sign. The meshed rung's one-shot dual read is the centralized analog of that live radial \(\mu\)-ascent — the same price, two solution paths.
  • With the 4Q-BESS present, the angle certificate still certifies on the uniform diamond (the device adds device-level variables only, never network constraints; the uniform residual shifts slightly, ≈0.0072). The device's reactive dispatch \(q[t]\) is whatever the SOCP itself chose, read post-hoc — no Volt-VAR droop or any other control law is imposed anywhere in the codebase (a deliberate anti-feature: the price mechanism, not a controller, allocates reactive power).

And an honest empirical finding: on this small, lightly-loaded, primarily-resistive fixture the reactive price is tiny relative to the active DADP (which sits close to \(\lambda_0\)) — reactive power simply carries very little marginal value at this optimum, and the dual reflects that down to the solver's numerical floor. The same is true in the radial live-\(\mu\) case: a near-zero \(\mu\) is an honest feature, and it makes an individual device's P–Q split inside its apparent-power cone non-unique (which is why cross-validations compare welfare, \(\lambda\), and \(\mu\), never a single device's \(q\) trajectory).

Honest caveats

  • The 4-bus diamond with two impedance profiles is the sole committed meshed evidence; a meshed-IEEE-13-with-tie-switch variant remains deferred.
  • On a mesh, an uncertified solution's welfare is an upper bound only; its duals should not be published as prices. The certificate tells you which regime you are in — it does not repair an unrecoverable solution.
  • The meshed rung is \(T = 1\), single-hour: it isolates the topology question from the intertemporal one.
  • The odd-cycle degeneracy is a property of this delegation path (the shared root pin of \(v\) and \(\hat v\) plus the exactness copy), documented and reproduced live — not a general claim about all meshed branch-flow formulations.

Where it lives / see it run

  • src/powerflow/ — MeshedFlow's delegation to ConvexBranchFlow.contribute!; MeshedFeeder in the core types.
  • certify_angle_recoverable! — the chord-aware angle-recovery certificate (diagnostics layer).
  • src/devices/FourQuadBESS.jl — the 4-quadrant BESS whose \(q\) makes :balance_q's dual economically live; src/admm/solve_admm.jl for the radial live \(\mu\)-ascent counterpart.
  • Docs page "Rung 10: Meshed Networks + Live Reactive Price" (docs/literate/meshed_reactive_price.jl), which reproduces the triangle infeasibility, both certificate verdicts, and the live reactive dual — all recomputed and self-checked at build time.

The Planning Layer: a Stackelberg–Nash Investment Game

From operations to planning: why investment needs a different game

Everything up to this point happened within a day: given the networks and devices that exist, the operational layer finds the welfare-maximizing dispatch and reads prices off the duals. Planning asks a different question: what should exist? Specifically, in the PSR N1–N2 setting the framework implements, two investments interact across the TSO–DSO frontier:

  • The distributor can invest in flexibility \(y_{inv}\) (batteries, aggregator enablement, control infrastructure). Flexibility does not reduce the total energy imported through the interconnection — it reshapes the import profile \(p_{import}[t]\), flattening the peaks that size the wire.
  • The transmission side must reinforce the interconnection corridor with capacity \(x_{inv}\) sufficient to carry whatever profile the distributor actually imports.

These decisions cannot be optimized independently, and they are not symmetric. The distributor moves first: it chooses its flexibility investment and its import profile \(z[t]\) anticipating that the transmission side will then reinforce at minimum cost to deliver exactly that profile. A peakier \(z\) forces more reinforcement; a flatter \(z\) (bought with flexibility investment) forces less. That anticipation structure — one player optimizing over the other player's optimal response — is a Stackelberg game, and it is a genuinely different mathematical object from the single-shot welfare maximization of the operational layer.

State the role assignment explicitly, because it is load-bearing for every sign convention below: the leader is the distributor (PSR note's N2 side, variables \(y_{inv}\), \(z\)); the follower is the transmission-reinforcement problem (N1 side, variables \(x_{inv}\), \(x_{op}\)). This assignment was not assumed from a reading of the note — it was empirically certified four ways in test/test_planning_certification.jl: the production Benders loop agrees with two structurally different BilevelJuMP MPEC single-level reductions of the same toy instance (StrongDualityMode and ProductMode) and with a hand-worked enumeration (\(y^* = z^* = 0.7\), leader cost \(-0.245\)), with no sign flip ever required. A fourth reformulation, BigMMode + HiGHS, is retained as a documented negative regression: the Big-M reduction of this instance's quadratic upper level is a genuine MIQP that HiGHS categorically cannot solve at any bound — itself a useful lesson in why MPEC reductions are kept as small-case oracles, never the production method.

The bilevel problem

Write the leader's problem with the followers' optimality embedded. The distributor chooses \(y_{inv}\) and the import profile \(z = (z[1], \dots, z[T])\) over a representative sub-horizon of \(T\) hours (e.g. the PV-peak hours), to minimize its total cost:

\[ \begin{aligned} \min_{\,y_{inv},\, z}\quad & c_y\, y_{inv} \;+\; \underbrace{\alpha_x(z)}_{\text{follower's optimal reinforcement cost}} \;-\; \underbrace{w(z)}_{\text{operational welfare at pinned } z} \\ \text{s.t.}\quad & 0 \le y_{inv} \le y_{max}, \\ & 0 \le z[t] \le y_{inv} \qquad t = 1,\dots,T, \end{aligned} \tag{P} \]

where both lower-level objects are optimal values of embedded optimization problems: \(\alpha_x(z)\) is the minimum cost at which the transmission follower can deliver the profile \(z\) (Section on the corridor follower), and \(w(z)\) is the optimal welfare of the full operational model from the earlier sections — network, aggregators, devices, MEM price \(\lambda_0[t]\) — with the frontier exchange pinned at \(p_{import}[t] = z[t]\). The box \(0 \le z[t] \le y_{inv}\) is the value-of-flexibility lever in one line: importing at hour \(t\) requires having invested enough flexibility-enabled capacity \(y_{inv}\) to carry it (the code deliberately uses the box \([0, y_{inv}]\), not \([-y_{inv}, y_{inv}]\): \(z\) is a physically nonnegative delivered import flow on this corridor).

Why bilevel \(\ne\) single-level. You cannot simply merge (P) with the followers' constraints into one big program: the leader is constrained not by the followers' feasible sets but by their argmin/optimal values. Replacing "\(x\) solves the follower's LP" with "\(x\) is feasible for the follower's LP" would let the leader pick a convenient non-optimal follower response — a different (and wrong) game. The two standard exact routes are:

  1. KKT / MPEC reduction: replace the follower by its KKT conditions (complementarity constraints), yielding a single-level Mathematical Program with Equilibrium Constraints — solvable via strong-duality equalities, complementarity products, SOS1, or Big-M linearization (this is exactly what BilevelJuMP automates). Exact, but the reductions blow up combinatorially, destroy convexity, and bury the duals you care about inside complementarity machinery.
  2. Value-function decomposition (Benders): keep the followers as intact subproblems, represent their optimal-value functions \(\alpha_x(\cdot)\) and \(-w(\cdot)\) in the leader's problem by epigraph variables supported from below by cutting planes, and iterate.

This framework uses route 2 — hand-rolled Benders, plus Gauss–Seidel diagonalization for the multi-distributor game — for three reasons that echo the whole project's philosophy: it is the thesis/PSR-note method (traceability), it scales (each iteration solves one LP master, one LP follower, and one already-validated operational model, instead of one monolithic MPEC), and it keeps the duals interpretable: the cut gradient \(\pi\) that drives convergence is itself the frontier price, as derived next. Route 1 survives as the certification oracle on tiny instances — the right division of labor.

The value-function / Benders reformulation, derived step by step

Step 1 — define the operational value function \(w(z)\)

Let \(\xi\) collect every operational variable (device schedules, network flows, voltages, frontier exchange), and let \(w(z)\) be the optimal welfare of the operational model with the frontier pinned:

\[ w(z) \;=\; \max_{\xi}\;\Big\{\, U(\xi) \;-\; \sum_{t=1}^{T} \lambda_0[t]\, p_{import}[t] \;:\; \xi \in \mathcal{F},\;\; p_{import}[t] = z[t] \;\; \forall t \,\Big\}, \tag{1} \]

where \(U(\xi)\) is the aggregate prosumer utility and \(\mathcal{F}\) is the same feasible set the operational layer already validated (power flow, voltage bounds, device constraints). This is not a new model: in code, build_planning_oracle (src/planning/subproblem.jl) reuses the operational layer's contribute! builders verbatim — same power-flow contribution, same aggregator contributions, same welfare objective shape (thesis eq. 3.38) — and adds exactly one new seam: \(z[t]\) as a genuine JuMP Parameter and a named constraint pin[t]: p_import[t] == z[t]. The model is built once; every Benders trial re-solves it via set_parameter_value. only. The same post-solve trust gates as the operational layer run before any dual is read — SOCP-exactness and battery-complementarity checks — and they are more load-bearing here, not less: the pin removes the priced-export degree of freedom that enables SOC exactness in the free welfare solve, so an off-optimal trial \(z\) is exactly the regime where the cone can go slack. A physically meaningless \(\pi\) from an inexact relaxation is refused (thrown), never returned as a cut gradient.

Step 2 — \(w\) is concave in \(z\), so \(-w\) is convex

Take \(z_1, z_2\) with optimal solutions \(\xi_1, \xi_2\) and any \(\theta \in [0,1]\). Because \(\mathcal{F}\) is convex and the pin is affine in \((\xi, z)\) jointly, the blend \(\theta \xi_1 + (1-\theta)\xi_2\) is feasible for the blended pin \(\theta z_1 + (1-\theta) z_2\); because the objective is concave in \(\xi\),

\[ w\big(\theta z_1 + (1-\theta) z_2\big) \;\ge\; \theta\, w(z_1) + (1-\theta)\, w(z_2). \]

So \(w\) is concave, and the leader's welfare-as-cost term \(v_{op}(z) := -w(z)\) is convex in \(z\). Convexity is what licenses cutting planes: a convex function is the pointwise supremum of its supporting hyperplanes, so a finite bundle of tangent cuts is always an under-estimate — the source of the Benders lower bound.

Step 3 — the optimality cut from the pin's dual (subgradient inequality)

Solve (1) at a trial \(z_k\) and dualize the pin with multiplier \(\mu\). The Lagrangian dual function

\[ g(\mu; z) \;=\; \max_{\xi \in \mathcal{F}} \Big\{ U(\xi) - \textstyle\sum_t \lambda_0[t] p_{import}[t] + \mu^\top (z - p_{import}) \Big\} \]

is an upper bound on \(w(z)\) for every \(\mu\) (weak duality for a max problem) and is affine in \(z\) with slope \(\mu\). At the solved trial, strong duality (the model is convex with interior) gives \(g(\mu_k; z_k) = w(z_k)\) for the optimal multiplier \(\mu_k\). Hence for all \(z\):

\[ w(z) \;\le\; w(z_k) + \mu_k^\top (z - z_k) \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad -w(z) \;\ge\; -w(z_k) - \mu_k^\top (z - z_k). \tag{2} \]

Equation (2) is a valid supporting hyperplane of the convex cost \(-w\) at \(z_k\) — the optimality cut. One implementation subtlety is worth stating honestly, because the code documents it as an empirical finding rather than an assumption: under JuMP's dual-sign convention for this Max-sense model, the raw dual.(pin) that the oracle returns is the negation of the naive \(\partial w / \partial z = \mu_k\) — i.e. it is directly \(\pi_k := -\mu_k \in \partial(-w)(z_k)\), the subgradient of the cost. The sign was pinned by a hand-derived monotonicity invariant (convexity of \(-w\) forces \(\pi\) to be non-decreasing in \(z\), crossing zero at the network's own unconstrained free-import optimum), and the four-way certification confirms it. The cut as implemented (add_optimality_cut!, epigraph :op) is therefore:

\[ \alpha_{op} \;\ge\; -w(z_k) + \sum_{t=1}^{T} \pi_k[t]\,\big(z[t] - z_k[t]\big), \qquad \pi_k = \texttt{dual.(pin)}. \tag{3} \]

Economic reading — the beautiful link. \(\pi_k[t]\) is the shadow price of the pin: the marginal cost to the distribution system of being forced to import one more unit at hour \(t\) instead of choosing its import freely. It is the same object the operational layer sells as a price — the frontier's locational marginal price, sitting next to the DADP that the oracle also reports (dadp = dual.(balance_p[agg_bus, :])). The duals-as-prices philosophy lifts intact from operations to planning: the quantity that coordinates the investment game is the linking price at the frontier, and the oracle additionally reports its duration-weighted reconciliation \(\pi_s = \sum_t \Delta t\, \pi[t]\) (reporting-only, never fed back into the optimization).

Step 4 — feasibility cuts from Farkas certificates

The master's box allows trials up to \(z[t] \le y_{max}\), which can exceed what the follower can ever deliver (\(\text{corridor\_cap} \cdot x_{inv}^{max}\)). At such a trial the follower LP is infeasible, and there is no cost or dual to cut with. What the LP solver returns instead is a Farkas certificate — a dual ray proving infeasibility. For the parametric LP \(\min\{c^\top x : \text{coupling } x_{op} = z,\ \dots\}\), infeasibility at \(z_k\) yields a ray along which the dual objective grows without bound; evaluating it gives a scalar \(v_k = \texttt{dual\_objective\_value} > 0\) (the "amount of infeasibility") and, restricted to the coupling rows, a vector \(u_k = \texttt{dual.(coupling)}\) measuring how that infeasibility responds to \(z\). Any \(z\) that is to remain feasible must satisfy

\[ v_k + \sum_{t=1}^{T} u_k[t]\,\big(z[t] - z_k[t]\big) \;\le\; 0. \tag{4} \]

Note the role of \(v_k > 0\): at \(z = z_k\) the cut reads \(v_k \le 0\), which is false — so the cut genuinely excludes the infeasible trial. The code enforces \(v_k > 0\) and finiteness in production, because a degenerate certificate would append a vacuous cut and silently cycle the master to iteration-cap exhaustion. Two deliberate implementation choices follow from the same requirement: solve_follower! calls optimize! directly, never through the escalating retry wrapper every other solve uses (retrying a genuine infeasibility would discard the certificate), and there is no penalized-slack shortcut — a locked decision: an "always feasible" softened follower would substitute a tuning parameter for a theorem.

Step 5 — the master problem, bounds, and the gap certificate

The master (build_master, src/planning/master.jl) is the leader's problem (P) with each value function replaced by an epigraph variable supported by its accumulated cuts:

\[ \begin{aligned} \min_{\,y_{inv},\, z,\, \alpha_{op},\, \alpha_x}\quad & c_y\, y_{inv} + \alpha_{op} + \alpha_x \\ \text{s.t.}\quad & 0 \le y_{inv} \le y_{max}, \qquad 0 \le z[t] \le y_{inv}, \\ & \alpha_{op} \ge -w(z_k) + \pi_k^\top (z - z_k) & \forall k \in \mathcal{K}_{op}, \\ & \alpha_x \ge \alpha_x(z_k) + \pi_{s,k}^\top (z - z_k) & \forall k \in \mathcal{K}_{x}, \\ & v_k + u_k^\top (z - z_k) \le 0 & \forall k \in \mathcal{K}_{feas}, \\ & \alpha_{op} \ge \underline{\alpha}_{op}, \quad \alpha_x \ge \underline{\alpha}_x . \end{aligned} \tag{5} \]

Three structural remarks. First, this is multi-cut Benders with two epigraphs — a deliberate departure from the PSR note, which needs only one \(\alpha\) (for the transmission cost) because it models the distributor's own operation as a linear term that sits directly in the leader's objective. Here the distributor's operation is a genuine convex welfare model, so it gets its own value function \(-w(z)\) and its own epigraph \(\alpha_{op}\). Second, the finite lower bounds \(\underline{\alpha}\) are declared at build time: without them the very first (zero-cut) solve has a free epigraph variable in a Min objective and returns DUAL_INFEASIBLE — a classic first-iteration Benders footgun avoided by construction. Third, the master is built once and cuts are appended as persistent rows to the live model handle; nothing is ever rebuilt inside the loop.

Now the bounds. Because the cut bundles are finite under-estimates of the true convex value functions, the master is a relaxation of (P):

\[ LB^{(k)} \;=\; \text{optimal value of (5) at iteration } k \;\le\; \text{optimum of (P)}. \]

Conversely, any follower-feasible trial \((y_k, z_k)\), evaluated exactly by actually solving both subproblems, gives a genuine achievable cost:

\[ \mathrm{cost}_k \;=\; c_y\, y_k \;+\; \alpha_x(z_k) \;-\; w(z_k) \;\ge\; \text{optimum of (P)}, \qquad UB^{(k)} = \min_{j \le k} \mathrm{cost}_j . \]

The loop (solve_stackelberg!, src/planning/benders.jl) alternates: solve the master (get \(LB\) and a trial \(z_k\)); solve the follower at \(z_k\) first (if infeasible, append cut (4) and continue — a feasibility cut never touches \(UB\), and the oracle is never solved at an undeliverable \(z_k\) where its exactness gates could throw); otherwise solve the oracle, append both optimality cuts, update the incumbent, and test

\[ \mathrm{gap}^{(k)} \;=\; \frac{UB^{(k)} - LB^{(k)}}{\max\big(1, |UB^{(k)}|\big)} \;\le\; \mathrm{tol}. \tag{6} \]

Since \(LB \le \text{opt} \le UB\), condition (6) is a certificate: the incumbent's true cost is within \(\mathrm{tol}\cdot\max(1,|UB|)\) of the bilevel optimum — not a heuristic stall test like a residual plateau.

The incumbent-vs-last-iterate subtlety. The code returns the incumbent \((y_{best}, z_{best})\) — the iterate that achieved the running-minimum \(UB\) — never the last iterate. The reason is easy to miss: convergence triggers when \(LB\) rises to meet an older iterate's \(UB\). The current iterate's own cuts have not yet tightened the master against it, so its true cost can exceed \(UB\) by an amount the gap does not bound. Only the incumbent carries the certificate \(c(y_{best}, z_{best}) = UB \le LB + \mathrm{tol}\cdot\max(1,|UB|)\).

The corridor follower: deliberately stylized transmission

The follower (build_follower, src/planning/follower.jl) is a minimal reinforcement LP:

\[ \alpha_x(z) \;=\; \min_{x_{inv},\, x_{op}}\; c_{inv}\, x_{inv} + \sum_{t=1}^{T} c_{op}[t]\, x_{op}[t] \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \begin{cases} x_{op}[t] \le \text{corridor\_cap} \cdot x_{inv}, \\ x_{op}[t] = z[t] \quad (\text{dual } \pi_s[t]), \\ 0 \le x_{inv} \le x_{inv}^{max}, \quad x_{op}[t] \ge 0 . \end{cases} \tag{7} \]

One corridor, one continuous investment variable, capacity proportional to investment. The coupling row's dual \(\pi_s[t]\) is the marginal reinforcement cost of the profile — the PSR note's \(\pi_s\), the same mathematical object, feeding the \(\alpha_x\) optimality cut directly. The model is continuous-only by enforced design: no binary or integer variable exists anywhere in src/planning/, and a permanent regression guards this (the PSR note's integer extension, problems 8–9, is a tracked deferral — see the scope section).

Why so stylized? Because it is PSR-note-faithful: the note itself poses the transmission side as generic linear investment/operation constraints, and the note's internal-network balance (its eqs. 1c/2c) is the one block deliberately not implemented — the corridor is a scalar aggregate, not a meshed grid. That asymmetry is intentional and honest: the research weight of this framework sits in the distribution-side operational model, which the note treats as an abstract linear balance and the implementation upgrades to the full validated SOCP welfare model. The follower is the mirror-image seam: a real transmission network (DC-OPF or better) drops into (7) without touching the Benders machinery, because everything the loop needs from the follower is its cost, its coupling dual, and its Farkas certificates — all of which any LP/conic transmission model provides. This is the natural upgrade path for a full N1–N2 implementation.

From one distributor to a game: Nash via Gauss–Seidel diagonalization

With \(N\) distributors importing through one shared corridor, no single bilevel problem describes the situation: each distributor \(i\) plays its own Stackelberg game against the transmission side, but the corridor capacity they draw on is common property. The solution concept is a Nash equilibrium among the leaders: a profile of decisions such that no distributor can lower its own cost given what the others do.

The shared corridor

build_shared_transmission (src/planning/coupling.jl) generalizes (7) to \(N\) distributors: each \(i\) owns its investment \(x_{inv}[i]\), its delivered flow \(x_{op}[i,t]\), and an individually-dualizable coupling row \(x_{op}[i,t] = z[i,t]\), while one pooled capacity row couples everyone:

\[ \text{capacity}[t]:\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_{op}[i,t] \;\le\; \text{corridor\_cap} \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_{inv}[i]. \tag{8} \]

Constraint (8) is the single genuinely new object of the multi-distributor layer: every distributor's flow competes for one aggregate capacity, and every distributor's investment contributes to it. Cost allocation is a modeling decision the PSR note leaves open; the implementation resolves it with per-distributor investment ownership — each \(i\) pays \(c_{inv}[i]\, x_{inv}[i]\) for its own reinforcement share — a documented, deliberate departure from a naive equal-split sketch, chosen because it is game-theoretically cleaner: each best response prices only its own investment, and the shared object is the aggregate capacity, not the cost split.

The best-response sweep

run_nash! (src/planning/nash.jl) computes the equilibrium by Gauss–Seidel diagonalization: sweep the distributors in order; for each \(i\), freeze everyone else's committed flows and investments, and let \(i\) solve its entire single-distributor Stackelberg–Benders problem — a full solve_stackelberg! convergence, with a DistributorView of the shared corridor standing in for a standalone follower — against that frozen background:

\[ \big(y_i, z_i\big)^{(k+1)} \;\in\; \arg\min \; \text{Stackelberg}_i\big(z_1^{(k+1)}, \dots, z_{i-1}^{(k+1)},\; \cdot\;, z_{i+1}^{(k)}, \dots, z_N^{(k)}\big). \tag{9} \]

Four mechanisms make this correct rather than merely plausible:

  1. Write-back timing (Gauss–Seidel, never Jacobi). Note the superscripts in (9): distributor \(i\) sees its predecessors' just-committed values from the same sweep. write_back! fires immediately after each best response converges — committing both the flow (as parameter values) and the investment (as pinned bounds) — before the next distributor is activated. The bound-pin on \(x_{inv}[j]\) matters: if a frozen neighbor's investment stayed a free variable, the active distributor could relax the pooled capacity row (8) using headroom it does not pay for — silently subsidizing itself from a neighbor's frozen decision.
  2. Fresh cuts per best response. Within one best response (fixed \(z_{-i}\)), distributor \(i\)'s follower value function \(V_i(z_i;\, z_{-i})\) is convex in \(z_i\), so cuts accumulated across Benders iterations remain valid — the single-distributor theory applies verbatim. But \(V_i(\cdot\,;\, z_{-i})\) is a different function for a different \(z_{-i}\): the capacity slack available to \(i\) shifts by exactly the change in \(\sum_{j \ne i} z_j\). A cut computed at an old \(z_{-i}\) is not merely loose for the new one — it can be actively wrong (non-supporting); a stale feasibility cut can exclude a \(z_i\) that became feasible once neighbors freed capacity. Every best response therefore starts its Benders master with an empty cut store — validity by construction, at a measured rebuild cost the trace instruments rather than hides.
  3. Nested tolerances, inner strictly tighter than outer. Each inner Benders tolerance must satisfy \(\mathrm{tol}_i < \mathrm{tol}_{outer}\), enforced as a hard ArgumentError, never merely documented. The outer loop declares convergence when best responses stop moving; if the inner solves were allowed noise at the same magnitude as the outer test, the outer residual could "converge" on solver noise rather than on a genuine fixed point.
  4. Optional damping \(\omega\). With \(0 < \omega \le 1\), the committed flow is \(z_i^{new} = \omega\, z_i^{BR} + (1-\omega)\, z_i^{prev}\) (\(\omega = 1\) recovers plain Gauss–Seidel, the default). When \(\omega < 1\) the follower is re-solved at the damped point so the matching investment is committed — pairing an undamped investment with a damped flow could leave the shared model infeasible for the next distributor.

Convergence definition. After each complete sweep, the outer residual is the worst-distributor movement \(\max_i \max\big( \lVert z_i^{(k+1)} - z_i^{(k)} \rVert_\infty,\; |\Delta x_{inv,i}| \big)\), and the loop stops when it falls below \(\mathrm{tol}_{outer}\) — the fixed-point test of (9), evaluated by one exported is_converged method so the reported criterion and the loop's actual test can never drift apart. Exhausting max_sweeps raises loudly; a non-converged result is never silently returned.

The honesty gate: never present one run as canonical

Gauss–Seidel diagonalization on a genuinely coupled game carries no general convergence or uniqueness guarantee. The framework does not paper over this — it instruments it. run_nash_probe repeats the entire diagonalization across a matrix of at least 3 initial-state seeds \(\times\) 2 sweep orders (forward/reverse), each run against a fresh corridor model (the lifecycle functions mutate bounds destructively, so reuse would leak state between runs), with every seed genuinely committed into the shared game state before sweep 1. Any non-converging combination raises — deliberately uncaught. Across all converged runs it reports the maximum pairwise spread of flows, investments, and total cost — never a mean, which could understate an outlier run — and its summary string is constructed to say "a converged equilibrium (spread: …)", structurally never "the equilibrium". A small spread is evidence of a well-behaved equilibrium at this calibration; it is presented as exactly that, not as a uniqueness proof.

Honest scope

The planning layer is a faithful, certified implementation of the PSR note's game structure — and a deliberately narrow one. Its known boundaries, stated plainly:

  • Continuous investment only. No binary/integer variable exists anywhere in src/planning/ (regression-enforced). The PSR note's integer extension — integer reinforcement with binary-expanded interconnection flow, solved via Lagrangian/integer L-shaped cuts in the SDDiP family (its problems 8–9) — is a tracked deferral (INT-STRETCH), not an omission.
  • A single stylized corridor. The transmission side has no internal network (the note's demand-balance blocks 1c/2c are the documented deliberate deviation); a real transmission model is the natural upgrade seam behind the follower's value-function interface.
  • Deterministic representative hours, not multi-year stochastics. The note weights everything by scenario expectations \(\tfrac{1}{S}\sum_s\); the implementation has no scenario index — each Benders iteration is a single deterministic trial over a representative sub-horizon (e.g. PV-peak hours), not an expectation, and there is no multi-year investment timeline or discounting.
  • A leader-side simplification. The note distinguishes generic distributor investment from flexibility-specific investment (\(y_{inv}\) vs \(y_{inv,flex}\)); the implementation collapses both into one \(y_{inv}\) — flexibility is the modeled investment.
  • The pv_boom finding. On the framework's own PV-boom case study, the multi-distributor probe converged to non-differentiated investments (\(x_{inv} = [0, 0]\)) at that calibration — the corridor economics simply did not separate the distributors — and this was reported as an honest negative finding rather than re-tuned until a difference appeared. An equilibrium result that fails to be interesting is still a result.

What a full N1–N2 implementation would add, in rough order of research value: a genuine transmission network inside the follower; scenario expectations (and eventually SDDiP-style integer cuts) in both subproblems; multi-year investment staging; and richer distributor heterogeneity so the Nash layer has genuine asymmetry to resolve.

Where it lives

  • src/planning/subproblem.jl — PlanningOracle: the build-once operational value function \(w(z)\) with the pin constraint and its dual \(\pi\) (the optimality-cut gradient), plus the exactness/complementarity trust gates.
  • src/planning/follower.jl — FollowerLP: the corridor reinforcement LP (7), its coupling dual \(\pi_s\), and the genuine Farkas-certificate infeasible branch.
  • src/planning/master.jl — BendersMaster: the two-epigraph master (5) with persistent optimality/feasibility cut rows and build-time epigraph lower bounds.
  • src/planning/benders.jl — solve_stackelberg!: the outer Benders loop, UB/LB/gap logic, incumbent tracking, and the follower-before-oracle ordering.
  • src/planning/coupling.jl — SharedTransmission, activate_distributor!/write_back!/DistributorView: the pooled corridor (8) and the best-response lifecycle.
  • src/planning/nash.jl — run_nash! (Gauss–Seidel sweep, nested tolerances, damping) and run_nash_probe (the multi-seed/multi-order honesty gate); NashTrace, the two-level convergence ledger.
  • src/planning/trace.jl — BendersTrace: the per-iteration UB/LB/gap ledger the convergence figures are drawn from.
  • test/test_planning_certification.jl — the permanent four-way BilevelJuMP/ hand-enumeration certification of the role assignment and sign conventions.

See it run

Two literate docs pages execute this machinery end-to-end during every docs build — the numbers on those pages are genuinely solved, never copied literals: "Rung 6 — Stackelberg-Benders (Planning)" (docs/literate/stackelberg_benders.jl) solves the certified-equivalent toy instance through solve_stackelberg! and draws the Benders bounds/gap figure from the recorded trace; "Rung 7 — Nash Diagonalization & Shared Corridor" (docs/literate/nash_diagonalization.jl) runs run_nash! and the full run_nash_probe on a symmetric \(N=2\) fixture, ending with the probe's own honest summary string and measured spread.

Running Experiments: the Declarative Harness

Everything in the preceding sections — formulations, devices, welfare solves, pricing, ADMM — is a builder. The experiment harness is the orchestration layer that turns those builders into a research workflow: declare what you want to run, run it reproducibly, store it with provenance, and sweep it across parameters. The harness adds no model and names no solver; it exists so that "the experiment" is a value you can hash, diff, and re-run bit-for-bit, instead of a script you hope you didn't edit.

The Scenario: primitives only, validated at construction

A Scenario is an immutable struct holding only primitive selectors — Symbol/Int/Float64/Bool/String — never a constructed feeder, aggregator vector, or price array: 

s = Scenario(name = "demo", feeder = :ieee13, strategy = :centralized, seed = 1, T = 24)

The fields fall into groups: identity and physics selectors (name, feeder ∈ (:ieee13, :ieee123), population, price, T, allow_export), the master seed, the strategy selector (:centralized or :admm), the ADMM knobs (\(\rho\), ε_abs/ε_rel, maxiter, τ_ratio, μ — ignored by the centralized branch, one flat schema), and additive mpc_* and stoch_* blocks consumed only by their own entry points (below).

The primitives-only rule buys three guarantees at once:

  • Validation is a construction invariant. The inner constructor throws a loud ArgumentError on any unknown selector or out-of-range value (feeder = :ieee14 never reaches a solver; \(\rho \le 0\) never reaches ADMM; stochastic probabilities must match the scenario count and sum to one). There is no half-configured state to debug later — a Scenario can never silently underdetermine a run.
  • Deterministic materialization. The heavy objects are rebuilt from the selectors + seed on every run (next subsection), so the spec fully determines the experiment.
  • Naming and provenance for free. Because every field is a DrWatson-friendly scalar, the on-disk artifact name (savename), hashing, and diffing fall out with zero customization. (One honest caveat: cumulative field growth across phases has pushed the fully descriptive default filename past Linux's 255-byte basename ceiling, so the storage layer truncates to a stem plus a stable content hash — a documented limitation, with no information lost because every selector is also stored inside the artifact.)

Materialization: from selectors + seed to a concrete problem

run_scenario first materializes the heavy objects deterministically: build_feeder(s.feeder) returns the IEEE-13 or IEEE-123 fixture; build_price(:mem, T, ...) returns the pinned 24-hour wholesale shape \(\lambda_0[t]\) (overnight trough, morning ramp, evening peak); build_population constructs the seeded residential aggregator population (thermostatic + deferrable + PV-battery per house). Randomness is disciplined by one helper: 

sub_seed(master::Integer, tag::Symbol) = Int(hash((master, tag)) % typemax(UInt32))

# :profiles and :population get independent, non-colliding deterministic sub-streams
profiles = generate_profiles(; seed = sub_seed(s.seed, :profiles), T = s.T)
aggs     = build_population(..., sub_seed(s.seed, :population))

Each consumer of randomness draws from its own freshly-seeded stable RNG derived from the master seed and a stream tag — never the global RNG. The same Scenario in the same process therefore reproduces bit-for-bit; changing only the seed changes only the seeded population (a feature the sweep example below exploits).

run_scenario: strategy dispatch, normalized result

After materializing, run_scenario dispatches on s.strategy — :centralized routes to solve_welfare + extract_dlmp, :admm to solve_admm — and normalizes both outcomes into one ScenarioResult: the welfare (thesis eq. 3.38), the DADP matrix \(\lambda_j[t]\) normalized to (n_load_nodes, T) with rows in ascending load-bus order for both strategies, the SOC-exactness certificate exact_maxgap, the ADMM-only fields (iters, final primal/dual residuals — missing for centralized), and a wall-clock elapsed that is recorded for reporting but deliberately excluded from every reproducibility comparison. run_scenario is path-free: it never writes a file.

A worked example

This mirrors the live docs page — every number there is produced by a real solve at docs-build time. First, the single declarative run:

s = Scenario(name = "docs-demo", feeder = :ieee13, strategy = :centralized, seed = 1, T = 24)
res_c = run_scenario(s)

res_c.welfare        # social welfare at the optimum (thesis eq. 3.38)
res_c.exact_maxgap   # max l·v − (P² + Q²) over all (branch, hour): tiny ⇒ duals are prices
res_c.dadp           # the DADP matrix λ_j[t], load buses × hours

The exact_maxgap read is worth pausing on: it is the certificate that the SOC cone is tight at the optimum, which is precisely the condition under which res_c.dadp is a physically meaningful price rather than the dual of a slack relaxation. The harness surfaces it as a first-class output on every run. Plotting a few nodal DADP curves against the wholesale price shows the pricing story of the whole framework in one figure — each \(\lambda_j[t]\) is the root price \(\lambda_0[t]\) plus that bus's network uplift:

Switching one field re-solves the identical materialized problem through the hand-rolled ADMM loop, landing in the same result schema: 

s_admm = Scenario(name = "docs-demo", feeder = :ieee13, strategy = :admm, seed = 1, T = 24)
res_a = run_scenario(s_admm)

res_a.iters, res_a.final_r, res_a.final_s        # dual-ascent convergence summary
abs(res_a.welfare - res_c.welfare) / abs(res_c.welfare)   # cross-strategy relative gap

Because both strategies emit the same (n_load_nodes, T) DADP shape, the decisive cross-validation — did the ADMM coupling price converge onto the centralized dual? — is a direct overlay:

Provenance: run_and_store

Persistence is a separate seam. run_and_store(s; dir) runs the scenario and @tagsaves a self-describing JLD2 artifact: 

res = run_and_store(s; dir = mktempdir())   # default dir: datadir("sims"), gitignored
fname = scenario_filename(s)                # the single source of truth for the artifact name

The saved dict carries every Scenario selector (so the artifact is self-describing without reconstructing the spec), the scalar results and the DADP matrix, the Julia version — and, stamped by DrWatson itself, the git commit of the code that produced it (plus the uncommitted patch if the tree was dirty, so even a dirty-tree run is reconstructible). The commit together with the committed Manifest.toml at that commit pins the entire package environment. Defensive details are handled for you: filenames use lossless float formatting (DrWatson's default 3-significant-digit rounding would silently collide two scenarios differing in a sub-percent ADMM knob) and safe = true appends _1, _2, … rather than ever overwriting a previous run.

Sweeps: run_sweep + collate_summary

A sweep is a Dict where vector-valued entries expand a Cartesian product and scalars stay fixed: 

params = Dict(
    :name     => "docs-sweep",
    :feeder   => :ieee13,
    :strategy => [:centralized, :admm],
    :seed     => [1, 2],
    :T        => 24,
)
results = run_sweep(params; dir = sweep_dir)          # 2 strategies × 2 seeds = 4 stored runs
df = collate_summary(sweep_dir, "docs-sweep.csv")     # one diff-friendly summary table

collate_summary reads every per-run artifact back into a single DataFrame/CSV under three deliberate rules — fixed column order, fully deterministic row order (sorted by every selector column, so no sweep shape can tie), and no machine-local path column (the git commit is kept as the provenance anchor) — so re-collating the same runs is byte-identical and the committed CSV never churns. The collated table feeds analysis directly:

The figure is the harness's whole argument in miniature: within a seed, the two strategies agree (the ADMM cross-validation holds across the sweep axis); across seeds, the welfare genuinely differs (the seed really does drive the population draw) — and every bar is reconstructible from a 16-character commit hash plus a Scenario.

run_mpc and run_stochastic: separate entry points, same schema

The two run-shape extensions read the same declarative Scenario but are deliberately not wired through run_scenario's strategy dispatch — they are independent entry points, so the validated day-ahead path stays byte-identical:

  • run_mpc(s) consumes the mpc_* fields (window length mpc_H, stride mpc_step, terminal-SOC toggle, bounded forecast-error magnitude) and drives a build-once receding-horizon window model — re-solved each step via JuMP Parameter injection — reporting rolling re-computed DADPs and an honest regret benchmark against a perfect-foresight day-ahead solve over the identical device set. Documented limit: the Deferrable device's construction-time energy window spans the full day and cannot live inside a short MPC window, so windows run Deferrable-excluded (the day-ahead benchmark side is matched accordingly).
